items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: When the House resumes on
Tuesday, 26 March the Government will l ook to progress the Student Loan Scheme
Amendment Bill (No 2), the Social Securi ty (Benefit Categories and Work Focus)
Amendment Bill, and the Local Electoral Amendment Bill (No 2). Wednesday is a
members’ day. As Thursday is the day befo re the Easter break, I would expect the
Business Committee to consider an earlier lifting time.
MOTIONS
Human Rights—International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination

items.speaker: Hon TARIANA TURIA
items.text: I seek leave to move a
motion without notice and wit hout debate concerning the International Day for the
Elimination of Racial Discrimination.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that course of action. Is there any objection?
There appears to be none. It can be so moved.

items.speaker: Hon TARIANA TURIA
items.text: I move, That this House note that today is the
International Day for the Elim ination of Racial Discrimination, and that it supports the
United Nations Secretary-General’s call th at we should recomm it to ending racial
discrimination and realising our vision of just ice, equality, and freedom from fear for
all.
Motion agreed to.
World Down Syndrome Day—Eighth Anniversary

items.speaker: MOJO MATHERS
items.text: I seek leave to move a motion without notice and
without debate on the eighth anniversary of World Down Syndrome Day.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that motion to  be put. Is there any objection?
There is none. The motion can be put.

items.speaker: MOJO MATHERS
items.text: I move, That this House note that today is the eighth
anniversary of World Down Syndrome Day, that it is the second time that the day has
been acknowledged under the auspices of  the United Nations, and that the House
recognise the contribution of New Zealanders with Down syndrome to our country and
communities.
Motion agreed to.
Economic Growth—GDP Growth for December 2012 Quarter and Unemployment
1. DAVID BENNETT (National—Hamilton East)  to the Minister of Finance :
What reports has he received on the economy?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Today Statistics New
Zealand has released the gross domestic pr oduct data for the D ecember 2012 quarter. It
shows that the New Zealand economy grew 1.5 percent in the quarter—the highest
quarterly growth since December 2009 and ab ove market expectations. Annual growth
was 3 percent year on year. The last time this was higher was before the global financial
8830 Questions for Oral Answer 21 Mar 2013
crisis and before the domestic recession that  preceded that crisis. This is a reasonably
encouraging result, particul arly when New Zealand’s 3 percent growth in 2012 is
compared with other countries: 1.6 percent in the US, 1.1 percent in Canada, 0.4 percent
in Japan, 0.3 percent in the UK, and negative 0.9 percent in the euro area.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What are the main drivers of GDP growth in the December quarter?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Statistics New Zealand reports broad growth, with 15 of the
16 measured industries growing in the December quarter. The main drivers of growth in
the December quarter were forestry, which grew 9 percent, the largest increase since
1999; retail accommodation and restaurants, up 2.3 percent, driven by retail activity;
wholesale trade, up 2.1 percent, driven by equipment and machinery sales; and
construction activity, up 1.8 percent, which was the fifth consecutive quarterly increase.
Manufacturing activity in the December quarter was up 2.7 percent year on year, but
down 0.5 percent in the quarter, and that wa s mainly due to a fall in oil production.
Household consumption increased 1.6 percent, and exports increased 2.1 percent.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What is the outlook for New Ze aland’s economic growth, and how
does that compare with other developed countries?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Treasury and the Reserve Bank forecast that New
Zealand’s economy can expect growth of 2 to 3 percent per year over the next 4 years.
This is in spite of the headwinds of ongoing uncertainty in the world economy, an
elevated exchange rate, deleveraging in th e household and Government sectors, and, of
course, this year’s drought. New Zealand’s forecast growth is higher than consensus
forecasts for the eurozone, Japan, the United Kingdom, and Canada. It is in line with
forecast growth in the United States of Amer ica and slightly below that of Australia.
There remains work to do, but this shows that New Zealand is broadly heading in the
right economic direction.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What are the risks to growth in th e next few years, and what steps is
the Government taking to manage these risks?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Although the world economy is showing some positive
signs, recent events in Europe and questio ns about the process of unwinding central
bank balance sheets shows th at some uncertainty does remain. That is why the
Government has focused on developing its Business Growth Agenda, a comprehensive
plan for building a productive and competitive economy and encouraging business
investment and growth, and also raising nati onal savings by getting back into surplus,
and developing new financial stability t ools, which include the macro-prudential
framework.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why is the Minister claiming the economy is performing well,
given that 23,000 people lost their jobs and 33,000 people left the workforce in the very
same December quarter that he has been referring to?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is worth pointing out to the member that, actually, in the
2 years to December, job growth in the qua rterly employment survey was 54,000 jobs. I
appreciate that, you know, we still have not  got a perfect economy, but if the member
wants to criticise the Government for achieving 1.5 percent growth in one quarter, I say
make him keep doing it.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Before he begins crowing a bout the temporary state of the
economy, will he tell the hundreds who queued outside a South Auckland factory 2
weeks ago, at Carter Holt Harvey’s Pakuranga factory, when they will get a job?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I do not think anybody has been crowing in this House
recently, except the right honourable member, but the reality of it is that the New
Zealand economy—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. What on earth could
that opening sentence have to do with an answer?
21 Mar 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 8831

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It was a very political question. I want to hear the—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: This is a political place.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is absolutely right. Could the Minister please complete the
answer.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. We were listening to
your response. We were having trouble hearing it because of the assistance you were
getting from the Associate Mini ster of Finance and the Lead er of the House. I do not
know whether there is something wrong with  the sound system, but , Mr Speaker, while
you were ruling, you were being overcalled by those two Ministers.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I did not hear a huge amount of in terjection, but I fully accept there
was some interjection. It goes to prove that interjection from either side of the House
when I am making a comment to any member will lead to disorder. Would the Minister
please now answer the question that was raised by the Rt Hon Winston Peters.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I was pointing out to the member that the only one
describing anything as crowing was the member himself. In terms of the job market, we
certainly accept that the j ob market remains challengi ng. Although there has been job
growth, it is not enough to ac tually meet the needs of all New Zealanders. That is why
the Business Growth Agenda is very, ve ry important in terms of encouraging
opportunities for investment in the New Zealand economy.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: It’s not working.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, actually, there are very strong signs that it is working
relative to the rest of the world. If the me mber would like me to run through again GDP
growth relative to the rest of the world for his benefit, I would be happy to do so.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Will the Minister explain to the country why foreigners are
coming here in their thousands on work permits, when a record number of young people
who are New Zealanders cannot get a job in their own country?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I find both of the legs of the question from the member
actually factually incorrect. Th e first leg of the question says that record numbers are
coming to New Zealand. Well, that is obvi ously not correct when you look at the
migration statistics—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. This Minister was
asked a straightforward question. The record numbers claim was to do with the record
numbers of youth out of work, and that is a fact. So would you ask him now to address
the question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Minister rose and straight away said he did not accept the
question that was put by the member, and that is a perfectly satisfactory answer.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: No, no—he claimed that I said that there were record
numbers of foreigners coming in on wo rk permits. I did not say that. The Hansard will
prove that. Now make him answer the question, as you are required to do.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member said that there were foreigners coming in in their
thousands. The Minister satisfa ctorily addressed that questio n by disputing that. He is
quite entitled to do so.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Will he answer the
question, then? Because he has not answered it yet.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: He did answer the question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: No, he did not. I raised a point of order on him, he
stopped—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And I ruled that the question had been answered. The Minister said
he just did not accept the supposition in the member’s question.
8832 Questions for Oral Answer 21 Mar 2013

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. With respect, if he
gets up and he claims I made a stat ement that I did not make, and the Hansard will
show it, how then can you avoid making him answer the question?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Because I have told the member that I am satisfied that the member
answered the question by saying he did not a ccept the suppositions that were raised by
the member in asking the question.
Government Financial Position—Current Account Deficit
2. Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance : Does he agree
with Westpac economist Nathan Penny that th e increase in the annu al current account
deficit to $10.5 billion, 5 percent of GDP, is  a “worrying symptom of New Zealand’s
two-speed economy and re-emerging imbalances”; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: A range of views have been
expressed on yesterday’s results, and not all the Minister would agree with. The
Minister would agree with Mr Penny, who al so said that the economy is clearly
improving and “household spending and busines s confidence are on the up.” But if Mr
Penny is concerned about the current account deficit now, then he must have been
apoplectic about it when the current accoun t deficit averaged over 8 percent under the
previous Government.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: If 30 percent of Mighty River Power shares being sold go
offshore, will this have a further negativ e effect on New Zealand’s current account
deficit?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: In terms of the first part of his question, there is no
indication that that is the case at all beyond Mr Cosgrove actually asserting it yesterday,
and we generally do not take advice from Mr Cosgrove in these matters. But in terms of
the member’s question with regard to invest ment and investment income, it all depends
on the quality of that investme nt income. I would point out to the member that in the
balance of payments yesterda y, if you look at the investme nt flows, there were two
main influences: New Zealanders were earn ing record amounts from their investments
offshore, which I think the member would ar gue was a good thing; also those that are
foreign investors investing in  New Zealand invested something like 60 percent of their
earnings back in the country, wh ich is also a good thing. The third thing is, to point it
out to the member, the actual investment  balances—yes, they were affected by
Government borrowing, and that is why th e Government is very, very focused on
getting back into surplus, which is something that his colleagues on the Opposition side
do not seem to understand.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: How can he credibly claim that his Government has rebalanced
the economy, which was its stated objectiv e, when there is double-digit housing
inflation in Auckland, persistently high une mployment, and a large current account
deficit?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, I would have a look at the GDP statistics today if I
was the member, which showed broad-base d growth across the New Zealand economy
in 15 of the 16 categories measured. The 16th was manufacturing. If you take oil and gas
out of that, manufacturing was also positive over the quarter and over the year. In fact,
the oil and gas one is the one, of course, that there is only one party in this House, or
perhaps also the parties that work alongside—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is not a necessary part of the answer.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why does he downplay the im portance of his failure to
rebalance the economy, when it is not just  the Westpac economist s but also the BNZ
economist Doug Steel who said that yesterda y’s current account numbers are “part of
the slippery slope that we think the external accounts are on,”?
21 Mar 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 8833

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is just, you know, incredul ous being lectured by that
member, because from 2005 to 2008 the balance of payments deficit was 8 percent of
GDP on average for the entire 3 years, so this Government is rebalancing the economy.
But the mess we were left with—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. That surely cannot be
within the Standing Orders—to get up, make no attempt to address the question, and
then start hammering on about some other pa rty’s record, which he is not responsible
for.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And it is certainly not desirable for the Minister to start with such a
personal attack. It is a politic al contest, but it would be helpful if Ministers would,
frankly, just answer the question.
Youth Employment—Youth Minimum Wage
3. CHRIS AUCHINVOLE (National)  to the Minister of Labour : What action is
the Government taking to improve work opportunities for young people?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: The passage of the Minimum Wage
(Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill today wi ll, from 1 May, create a wage for 16 to
19-year-olds entering the workforce, coming off a benefit, or undertaking training.
Young people who do not successfully move into work or who are unemployed for long
periods face a real risk of long-term unemp loyment. The starting-out wage will provide
an incentive for employers to help give young people a foot in the door and start
building their skills and experience.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: How have young people been a ffected by the recession and
current wage settings?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Young people have been more negatively affected—
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Young people have been more negatively affected in
employment terms by the recession than olde r workers. The minimu m wage settings of
the Labour Government did not help. The new entrants wage it established is estimated
to have cost up to 9,000 jobs and is cu rrently being used by only 2 percent of
employers. This Government wants New Zealanders who are able to work to do so. The
starting-out wage will help set young pe ople up for a lifetime of meaningful
employment.
Solid Energy—Financial Position and Accountability
4. Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE (Labour)  to the Minister for State Owned

items.speaker: Enterprises
items.text: Does he stand by all statements he  and his Ministeria l colleagues have
made regarding State-owned enterprises?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: on behalf of the

items.speaker: Minister for State Owned Enterprises
items.text: Within the context they were made the
Minister stands by all his st atements. In regard to the likely hundreds of statements
made by 20-plus ministerial colleagues in re lation to all State-owned enterprises over 5
years, that is just a little bit difficult to check out in 3 hours’ prep time.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Does he agree with the Prime Minister that an inquiry into
Solid Energy will not achieve anything even though $389 million of taxpayers’ money
is in jeopardy and over 400 miners and associated staff have lost their jobs?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Yes, the Minister agrees with the Prime Minister. The
issues that Solid Energy has had in regard to  its business over the last couple of years
are very well traversed and th ere are some excellent articles in the media the member
might like to read to assist with that. The focus of the Government is on working
8834 Questions for Oral Answer 21 Mar 2013
through the situation with the Solid Energy board and management to maximise the
outcome for the company.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: In the absence of an inquiry in to the near collapse of Solid
Energy, where hundreds of miners and associat ed staff have lost their livelihoods,
where $389 million worth of taxpayers’ money is in jeopardy, and where he did nothing
to stop this from happening, how does he expect the public to have confidence in him as
Minister for State Owned Enterprises when  under his watch an export award - winning
company has been driven into the ground?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I appreciate that that was a ve ry politically loaded question
from the member, but the answer—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: It was a factual question; just answer it.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No, it is not a factual questi on, actually, but the answer in
terms of the position of the Minister for State Owned Enterprises, as the member
knows, is that the responsibility for the i nvestment decisions made by the company fall
to the board and management, a nd the responsibility for coal pr ices actually falls to the
world market.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: In the absence of any inquiry into the near collapse of Solid
Energy, where hundreds of miners and associat ed staff have lost their livelihoods and
$389 million worth of taxpayers’ money is in  jeopardy, and where, again, he did
nothing to stop this happening, how does he expect the public to have confidence in his
ability to restore Solid Energy to the export award - winning company it once was under
the previous Government?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I suspect Mr Cosgrove is cl aiming responsibility for world
coal prices.
Hon Damien O’Connor : Does the Minister support the National Party members
who blocked an inquiry into Solid Energy; and how can employees have any confidence
in their future if the Government refuses to investigate what has gone wrong inside the
company in the last few years?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am reasonably new here, but I understand select
committees are in charge of their own des tiny. The member and his colleague are on
that select committee. I take it they were unable to persuade th eir colleagues of the
merits of an inquiry.
Immigration, Parent Category—Allocation of Visas
5. DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) to the Minister of Immigration: Does he stand
by his statements made in Question Time on 12 March 2013?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Yes.
Denis O’Rourke: How can the Minister assert “This Government is colour-blind and
not designed to favour any nationality over a nother.”, when in the year ending June
2012 parents admitted from China were more than 120 percent of skilled immigrants
from China, while parent immigration from other countries did not exceed 24 percent of
skilled immigrants?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I stand by the answer to that question, which is
that every single one of the residents who qualified under the pare nt category did so
because they met the criteria. But in resp ect of the comparison between the proportion
of those accepted in a year under the parent category relative to the same countries’
skilled migrants, I should point out that the parent category applicants generally come at
least 5 years after their children are accepted under the skilled migrant category, and the
comparison is completely flawed.
Denis O’Rourke : In view of the Government’s  2012 policy change designed to
rebalance the parent category, will the Minister now give an assurance that parent
21 Mar 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 8835
category numbers from China will not exceed  the number of skilled immigrants from
China in the current year?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Well, I reiterate the assurance that I gave last
week, which is that ever ybody who comes in under that category will do so because
they meet the criteria. But I note that in the 8 months since those new criteria have taken
effect, the proportion of Chinese parent cat egory visas that have been approved has
nearly halved and that the proportion of a pprovals from other countries has gone up.
That is as a consequence of the changed criteria.
Denis O’Rourke : If, as the Minister says, “last year we made changes to give
priority to migrants who can make a real contribution”, will he adopt the New Zealand
First policy to cap parent category migrants from each country to 20 percent of the
skilled migrants from that country?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: No, I will not give that assurance. I note for the
benefit of the colleague sitting beside the member, Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor,
who tweeted during last week’s question tim e, “Why is National giving priority to
Chinese over Pacific Islanders?”, that the coun try with the highest proportion of parent
category visas related to skilled migrant visas is Samoa.
Public Transport, Auckland—City Rail Link
6. JULIE ANNE GENTER (Green) to the Minister of Transport: Has he read the
City Centre Future Access Study which found that, of the options for Auckland CBD’s
transport infrastructure, the City Rail Link “has the highest road network speeds within
the City Centre”?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Yes, I have, but I am not
sure that the member has correctly interpreted this research. The city rail loop would not
be part of the road network. From a road safe ty perspective, I would ask that she please
not drive her car along railway lines.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: Given his focus on reducing travel time for New Zealand
motorists, why is his Government blocki ng progress on the city rail link, which will
reduce rail journey times by as much as 60 pe rcent and result in faster travel times for
hundreds of thousands of Auckland motorists?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: We are not blocking progress on the rail loop. We are
in discussions with Auckland Transport and Auckland Council on what are the best
options for them moving forward. What we do k now is that even if the rail loop were to
be built, by 2030 the congestion situation in Auckland would be no better than it is now.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: Is he denying that building the city rail link would give much
better transport options to tens of thousands of Aucklanders in 2030?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: How will the Government provide adequate transport options
for the 100,000 people who will be commuting to  Auckland’s central business district
every weekday by 2021 if he continues to say no to the city rail link, which will move
the most people the fastest with the least congestion?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Even if the city rail loop were in place right now, it
would have minimal effect on the total numbe r of journeys into the city by cars by
2021. The reality is that either way, you ar e looking at an increased number of cars
coming into the central city, so simply saying  “Let’s build this $2.4 billion rail loop to
overcome a problem.” is not recognising what the problem is.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: I seek leave to table this graph from Auckland Transport,
showing that the number of people travelling by car entering Auckland central business
district from 2001 to 2012 re duced significantly, by 20 percent, while the number
coming by public transport increased by 50 percent.
8836 Questions for Oral Answer 21 Mar 2013

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: What is the source of the document?

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: This is data provided by Auck land Transport to myself. I do not
believe it is publicly available.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that. Is th ere any objection? There is not. It
can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: Does he disagree with the recommendation of the Government-
commissioned Enright report on New Zealand’ s competitiveness, which stated that the
Auckland rail link must be the priority to improve productivity; if so, why?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I neither agree nor disagree . What we are doing at the
moment is trying to work out whether or not that rail  loop should progress, and,
secondly, if it were to, what would be the opt imal time for it to pr ogress. I would point
that, counter to what the member has just said about the reduced number of journeys
into the city in 2021 should that rail loop go ahead, my information suggests it would be
around about a 1,600 reduction—not the numbers the member is claiming.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: How many more reports does he n eed to conclude that the city
rail link is necessary, given that we have ha d the Enright report, the City Centre Future
Access Study, and the 2010 Auckland city rail link business case, before he will get on
board with this project that the people of Auckland and the businesses of Auckland
want?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: There is the problem, you see. Here is the report that
the member speaks to—a very large volume. It is accompanied by many other large
volumes, and they do not, either individually or collectively, reach the conclusions she
claims. This is a $2.4 billion pr oject, in today’s terms, for a relatively short piece of rail
for very modest gains.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: I seek leave to table this page from the Enright report, which
states that the Auckland city rail link should be a priority for lifting productivity—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is the Enright report available to members?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It is. Then it will not be tabled.
Information and Communications Technology Sector—Jobs
7. CLARE CURRAN (Lab our—Dunedin South)  to the Minister for Economic

items.speaker: Development
items.text: What contribution, if any, will the ICT sector make to the Government’s
stated 2011 Budget commitment to 170,000 net new jobs being created by 2015?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: According to
projections released by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment—and it is
important to point out that these are neve r exact numbers, because you are asking for
individual occupational groups —the computing professionals’ sector is expected to
grow by 8,000 in the 2010-15 period, an annual growth rate of 4.4 percent, the highest
of any profession. My hope is that that grow th will be larger, based on the anecdotal
experience of a lot of people looking for information and comm unications technology
professionals at the moment. Orion Health , which recently created 100 new jobs, has
said it is a very tight market, and that if it could find more people, it would mean more
development. It said that if it cannot find the people, “we will have no choice but to hire
people elsewhere.” The Government recognises the potential the information and
communications technology sector has to grow the New Zealand economy, which is
