MINIMUM WAGE (STARTING-OUT WAGE) AMENDMENT BILL
Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I move, That the Minimum Wage
(Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill be now read a third time . It gives me great
satisfaction to support this bi ll at its third reading. This bill delivers on the
Government’s commitment to establish a starting- out wage to assist young people to
gain a foothold in the labour market. I woul d like to thank the Tr ansport and Industrial
Relations Committee, officials, and submitte rs for their work on, and contribution to,
this bill.
21 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8861
The Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage ) Amendment Bill is part of the
Government’s focus to create job oppor tunities for young people who are finding it
difficult to get work in the current economic climate, and who have not been helped by
the minimum wage settings broadened by the previous Government. The youth
minimum wage was abolished in 2008 by the Labour Government and replaced by a
new entrants wage that was rarely us ed. Research commi ssioned by the then
Department of Labour suggests the aboliti on of the youth minimu m wage has resulted
in the loss of up to 9,000 jobs for young Ne w Zealanders. The new entrants wage
applies for the first 3 months or 200 cumu lative hours. Businesses complain it is too
complicated, impractical, and fleeting to bot her with. Ministry of Business, Innovation
and Employment research indicates it is used by only 2 percent of employers.
The starting-out wage will encourage empl oyers to take on young people, who will
then have the satisfaction of earning mone y, gaining skills, and getting the work
experience they need. The bill achieves this by providing the ability to set different
minimum wage rates, known as starting-ou t wage rates, by Order in Council for
specified groups of young people aged 16 to 19 y ears. These rates must be set at no less
than 80 percent of the adult minimum wage. This bill encourages continuity with the
same employer by providing that a young pers on on a starting-out wage must complete
6 months of continuous work with an employer before they are entitled to be paid the
adult rate by the employer. With a steady work history behind them, young people, like
other employees with a steady work history, will be seen as less risky for new
employers to take on.
The bill also addresses the problem of young people who have been on a benefit for a
length of time of 6 months or more and may face difficulty re-entering or gaining a
foothold in the workforce. The bill will provide for a starting-out wage rate to be set for
these young people, and in so doing encourag e employers to take on young people who
have been out of the workforce for a while or may lack skills or experience. The bill
also provides for young people aged betw een 16 and 19 years w ho are required to
undergo training as a condition of the work to be paid the starting-out wage, rather than
the minimum training wage.
This Government is committed to creating an environment that encourages economic
growth. Part of this environment is providi ng a better balance to our labour market
rules, which focuses on helping businesses grow while ensuring workers’ rights and
opportunities are maintained. In itiatives such as the star ting-out wage will give young
people the opportunity to get a foot in the door . This bill will provide a strong incentive
for employers to take on young people. Once in work, young people will gain the
essential and necessary skills and work experi ence that will assist them throughout their
working lives. This is a positive step fo r young people in New Zealand. I commend this
bill to the House.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I rise to put on record  Labour’s very strong
opposition to the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill. The passing of
this bill today will create an underclass of young workers and consign them to economic
marginalisation. Not content with making it impossible for young workers to challenge
their unfair treatment and dismissal in the fi rst 90 days of employment, and not content
with its abject failure in addressing yout h unemployment, this Government has now
come up with a failed and tired old approach of cutting the wages of young workers
aged 16 to 19 years.
This bill assumes that there are thousands of employers out there just waiting to offer
jobs to younger people and to give them a foot in the workforce, as National says and as
the Minister of Labour says. We know that that is a false assumption. The Ministry of
Business, Innovation and Employment has openly admitted that it has very little idea of
8862 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 21 Mar 2013
whether this bill will meet it s stated outcomes. The ministry  tried a best guess that this
bill could create 400 to 1,100 jobs, but we in Labour have learnt to become very wary of
Government predictions of job creation. Who has forgotten the 2011 Budget projection
of 170,000 new jobs by 2015-16? What has ha ppened since then? Unemployment has
continued to rise, more good jobs have b een lost, and our youth unemployment is a
national disgrace. Then today we learnt that  there could be as many as 1,500 more jobs
going from Telecom, which are high-skilled jobs.
What worries me most of all about this bill is that it is just the beginning under this
young, new Minister. Treasury has suggested that paying other workers sub-minimum
wages is something that could be extended in the future—other workers who have a
high unemployment rate. So what we could s ee in the future are the vulnerable workers
such as M āori and Pasifika or those who live in areas where j obs are hard to find on a
so-called starting-out wage.
Unfortunately, what this bill does is remind us that the Government has no ideas and
that we are going back to the past, wher e low-wage jobs we re the norm, where
productivity was increased by having more people paid less and working longer, where
good jobs were offshored because of lack of investment and hands-on economic policy,
and where our young people were sacrificed to a future of economic marginality.
This bill needs to be read in context with  the Government’s planned changes to other
employment laws, which will help slash the wages for hundreds of thousands of other
New Zealand workers. From what I hear, the Government’s ideas for those employment
law changes are so irrational that the Mini stry of Business, Innovation and Employment
is struggling to draft the appropriate legislation. I think that that may be why the former
Minister of Labour Kate Wilkinson faile d to progress the National Government’s
policy, and the new, young, much-admired but very inexperienced and naive Minister
Simon Bridges will find the same thing.
Cuts to workers’ rights and pay are classic National Party. In the face of its economic
failures and its marginalisation of thousa nds of unemployed and underemployed, it has
resorted to its tried and fa iled policies of last centu ry. In 2010 National strongly
opposed Roger Douglas’ member’s bill to reintroduce youth rates, and the then Minister
of Labour, Kate Wilkinson, confirmed that her Government would not support a return
to discriminatory and unfair youth rates. We heard a range of florid speeches—and I can
see that we are going to ge t another one from members like David Bennett and Jackie
Blue—opposing youth rates and sa ying that young people deserved better. Well, what
has changed? What has changed is that the Government is returning to its neo-liberal
roots of making cuts to worker s’ rights and pay as a substi tute for real economic policy
and plans, and it is our young people who are going to pay the price.
You know, the most offensive thing about th is bill is its framing as a starting-out
wage. We know that that title is simply not true. Under this bill 16 and 17-year-olds will
be returned to youth rates every time they st art a new job, regardless of previous job
experience, and under this bill 18 and 19-yea r-olds, who may have already had jobs on
adult minimum wages or adult wages, will be  forced on to sub-minimum rates if they
have been unfortunate enough to be on a social  security benefit, including the invalids
benefit and sickness benefit. This bill, combined with the social welfare reforms from
the Minister for Social Development, Paul a Bennett, that we heard about and debated
here yesterday, feeds the noti on that our young people are l azy, they are addicted to
drugs, and they are unreliable.  It is based on the false as sumption that the only way we
can get young people into work is to pay them less.
The National Government has tried to run th e argument that this bill is about the
dignity of work. Labour certainly  agrees that work is the be st antidote to poverty, but it
should be decent work. Decent work is not where people are paid less than they are
21 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8863
worth, where they can be sacked without reason,  where they can be forced to take jobs
that could be unsafe, and where they are puni shed by a nasty regime  within the social
security system if they do not gratefully sign up for any job on a sub-minimum wage. A
job should not only be about the work performed. It is a lot more than that. It is about
getting experience, but also it is about relatio nships with other people in the workplace.
It is about being fulfilled as a human being. People must feel recognised for their efforts
and know that they are valued for those effo rts and the contribution they make, and that
applies to 16 and 17-year-olds and to 18 and 19-year-olds as much as it does to anyone
else.
What this bill will do is unleash thousands of young people available as cheaper
workers on to our labour market , and that affects every single worker in New Zealand.
There is absolutely no doubt that havi ng cheaper young workers leads to the
displacement of older workers—older workers who, in this dire ec onomic climate, are
desperate to hang on to their jobs, who are not only in the queues of unemployment but
also underemployment, who are crying out fo r better wages, and who are crying out for
a Government that will do something to help them. And it takes no account of the
expenses of young people—the expenses th ey incur while act ually working—and
whether the job will pay for the expenses of going to work.
When we have a Minister for Social De velopment who is so desperate to claim
success in job creation that she trumpets th e employment of 16 workers for 2 weeks in
the census collection, we are in real trouble.  When we now apparently have a culture
within our Government agencies where job gains are celebrated by the ringing of a bell,
no matter what the job is, no matter what the pay level is, no matter what the conditions
are, and no matter what the safety risks are,  and where all that matters is numbers, we
are in serious trouble.
As we have gone through this bill, I have had on my mind one person I want to
mention, and that is a teenager called Peni ata Junior Endermann. He is a student at
Edgewater College in Auckland who works fr om 5 p.m. to 10 p.m., Monday to Friday,
as a cleaner earning the minimum wage. He is studying full-time. He is still at school.
He is 16 going on 17. This job, along with his homework, means that Peniata puts in 16-
hour days to help his mother, who also works as a cleaner on the minimum wage, and to
help provide for his family and three siblin gs aged 15, 13, and 9. So Peniata is not lazy
or unmotivated or unwilling. He has got hims elf a job. He should not  have had to, but
the state of our economy and low wages mean that in families like his everyone has to
help out. But if Peniata changes his employ ment or if he is employed by a different
cleaning firm, under this bill and the Gove rnment’s intentions around protections for
cleaners and other vulnerable workers, hi s pay will go down to $11 an hour. So it is
young people like Peniata whom the young Minister Simon Bridges needs to talk to.
This Government did not listen to the mo re than 500 submissions opposed to this
bill. It ignored the business community, who said  that this is not a silver bullet and will
not do the job and that the Government needs to do a lot better on youth unemployment.
The simple arrogance of this bill is gobsmacking. I cannot express strongly enough
Labour’s disappointment and dismay at the direction this Government is taking today.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: What a bizarre and
shambolic contribution that wa s from David Bennett. He st arted off talking about the
Australian Labor Party. He is so embarrassed  by this piece of legislation, the Minimum

But I have got to be hones t, I like quoting David Benne tt. My favourite one, from a
few years ago, is: “The Government is not here  to make your life be tter.” That was my

But that is not all. David Bennett has had a range of views on this issue. A mere 2

in the House to look at this issue in the wide r perspective of what we want to achieve in

opportunities will necessarily be provided.” David Bennett, take a bow. I could not

It was not just David Bennett; it was Jackie Blue as well, I think, at the time. Paula

This National Party flip-flops all over the pl ace. It was in favour of it when it was in
Opposition, then it was opposed to it when it was in Government. Now, a couple of
years later in Government, it is in favour of it again. It is all at sea. What an absolute
shambles this Government is.
Let us be real about what this  bill truly represen ts. It represents the failure of this
Government. It represents the failure of the National Government to grow the economy.
It represents the failure of the National Gove rnment to create more jobs. It represents
the failure of the National Government to keep  people in education, to make sure there
are places available at universities and at pol ytechnics and in apprenticeships. It is an
absolute demonstration of what happens when a Government comes to power with
absolutely no economic plan at all.
So what we have got is people losing j obs at Telecom, in the productive sector,
people losing engineering jobs, and people lo sing high-skill, high- wage jobs, so now
more and more of those people are competing with youngsters for those entry-level jobs
at McDonald’s, at Burger King, at Wendy’s, at Pak ’N Save, at Countdown. That is the
real problem here. Those jobs, which should be the entry-level jobs and often are the
minimum wage jobs, are the jobs where, basically, youngsters were the only people
applying for them. Now young people face massive competition from people who have
been turfed out of their jobs because this economy is so weak.
And, look, we accept that there is a certain nature of evolution in the job market.
Some jobs will come and some will go. Some  industries will rise, some businesses will
rise; others will fall. But as businesses fall, if the economy is in good health, there will
be other jobs for people to go to. There will be other high-skill, high-wage jobs for
people to go to. But no, the only places wher e there are new jobs are the fast-food and
supermarket industries, which is why this bill, the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage)
Amendment Bill, is being passed by this Government—because young people are
having to compete so hard against the olde r workforce for those low-skill, low-wage
jobs.
What happened to the aspiration? What happened to the brighter future?

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What happened to Julia Gillard?

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: Where did it all go? It has all gone to Australia. That is
right—they have all flown to Australia. Members opposite can say what they like about
what is happening with the Australian G overnment at the mo ment, they can say
whatever they like, but the Australians ar e taking our talented young people. People are

of somebody else who is doing the same job as them and is just a couple of years older.
That is unjustifiable discrimination. This  House has been doing a very good job of
dealing with other forms of unjustifiable disc rimination in the past few weeks, and yet
here the National Government is reintroduci ng another form of absolutely unjustifiable
discrimination.
The fact is that the thing the Government sa ys this bill is supposed to achieve, which
is to give young people a supposed leg-up by al lowing them to get into a job at a lower
wage rate, already exists. It already exists, and yet we still have massive youth
unemployment, we still have no growth in jobs, and we still have  no growth in the
economy. So doing more of what we have al ready got is not going to change things.
That is the real situation. This bill is si mply a representation of this Government’s

Under National’s watch 72,000 young New Zealanders aged between 18 and 30 have

John Key has lost his ambition. He has lost the vision for a brighter future. He is

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard

our country being a place of low wages a nd low opportunity, and people are leaving in

You do not improve the lot of our future generations by paying them less for doing

working for this country’s future? Th is Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage)
Amendment Bill demonstrates how this sh ambolic National Government has failed
New Zealanders, failed our young people, and failed to grow the economy. The sooner

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: I think we can probably agree in the House today that
there is no doubt that we should be very worried about the rate of youth unemployment
21 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8867
in New Zealand. We know that there ar e at least 90,000 young pe ople nationwide who
are not in any kind of employment, education, or training. We know that in every region
of the country more young people are claiming the unemployment benefit than 5 years
ago. We know that youth unemployment for those aged 15 to 19 is at around 30 percent.
That is a rate that rivals  those of Spain, of Greece, an d of all those countries in
economic chaos at the moment. We do not want to be in that list of countries. As well as
hurting our young people right now, such high rates of youth unemployment will be
disastrous for our country in the long te rm—for our long-term health, education,
employment, and justice spending and for th e skills and sustainability of our future
workforce. So this issue does deserve the highest priority of this House.
However, the Government claims that reintroducing youth rates is its answer to these
high rates of youth unemployment—that reintroducing youth rates, as it does in this bill,
the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage ) Amendment Bill, will improve job
opportunities for young people and will encour age employers to take on more young
workers. So how did it arrive at this pa rticular solution to the problem of youth
unemployment? Did it conduct a detailed evalua tion of all the different ways that you
might address youth unemployment, of all the different options to help young people
into employment and training, and have a look at those against some kind of robust
criterion about which was the most likel y to succeed? No, it did not. It made an
ideological commitment before the election to reintroduce youth ra tes—largely at the
behest of that single-membe r, irrelevant, and unpopular su pport party that it has, the
ACT Party—and pursued it, without even look ing at any other opti ons to reduce youth
unemployment.
How do we know it did not look at any othe r options? Because it says so in the
regulatory impact statement for this bill. I quote: “The star ting out wage proposal is a
pre-election policy commitment. The Ministry’s  analysis has theref ore not considered
other options for achieving the objectives of  the proposed starting out wage package.”

items.speaker: That is right
items.text: it did not ev en look at any other options to achieve th e objective of
reducing youth unemployment. This is not evidence-based policy.  It is—to borrow a
phrase that I learnt last w eek from my colleague who ha s just spoken, Iain Lees-
Galloway—policy-based evidence. Having come  up with the policy,  it then got its
officials to come up with some evidence to support it. That is no  way to make policy,
and what is in this bill is no way to reduce youth unemployment.
Before I go on to talk a bit about the pr ovisions of the bill and how harmful and
discriminatory they are, I want to spend a little bit of time talking about some of the
other things that the Government coul d do to assist more young people into
employment, education, and training, instead of what is in this bill. The reason I want to
do that is that I am aware that there are probably quite a few young people following the
debate today, and they will have heard a lot if they are listening—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Really? Really?

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: Yes, because they are directly affected by it, Mr Bridges.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: I doubt it.

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: They will have heard—and if th ey are not listeni ng, there is a
reason for that. They will have heard how hopeless the youth unemployment situation is
and how they should be satisfied with any paid  job they can get—even if it is paid at
less than subsistence wages. They will have he ard a lot about how bad the bill is, and it
is very bad. But I do not want any young people listening to this debate to lose hope or
lose faith in the ability of this Parliament  and us as MPs to advocate for them and for
policies that actually work for them. I woul d not blame them if, having heard all that
doom and gloom, they switch off. And if, inde ed, as the Minister of Labour says, they
are not watching—and he, as th e Minister responsible for this bill, should be very
8868 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 21 Mar 2013
concerned if they are not—it is because politics has become  irrelevant and hostile to
them. Indeed, the voting statistics from the last election show that more and more young
people are doing exactly that —turning away from Parl iament and politics and
disengaging from our political system. It is b ecause of bills like this that they are doing
that.
I want to assure young people that some of us  at least have ideas and solutions to put
on the Table and a genuine commitment to engage with young people about what works
best for them. Had the Government done that for this bill, I think it would look very
different. The Green Party, for example, is committed to better pathways to
employment, education, and training for young people, including more equitable access
to student support for higher education; gr eater investment in apprenticeships—even
more than the Government has recently made, which is nowhere near enough—greater
investment in job placements and partners hips with businesses and employers; and
better financial support for young job seekers.  The Transport and Industrial Relations
Committee heard many practical ideas about how to achieve these things from the
young people who submitted on this bill, w ho were full of good ideas about how we
could address the problem of youth unempl oyment. Sadly, they were ignored by the
select committee. They were ignored by the select committee, like all but seven of the
over 500 submissions that were received by the committee. Out of those over 500
submissions, most of them—over 500 of  them—were opposed, and only seven
submissions were in favour of the bill. Ye t the Government went with the seven, not
with the 500.
Why were those 500 submitters opposed to th is bill? Well, I will tell you. It is
because it introduces unacceptable discrimination into our law. I have said this in the
first reading and in my second reading speech. It is not acceptable in our country any
more to pay women less than men for doing the same job. It is illegal to do that. It might
still happen, but if it does, we do our best to find out about it and prosecute. Similarly, it
is not acceptable to pay people from ethnic mi norities less than others for doing exactly
the same job. It is illegal, and when that ha ppens we do our best to prosecute and report
it. Similarly, it is not acceptable to pay young people who are doing the exact same job
as older workers less for the same job. Sin ce 2008, thanks to a member’s bill in the
name of the former Green MP Sue Bradford, it has been illegal to do that too. But this
bill reverses that change and reintroduces  lower minimum wages fo r three categories of

19-year-olds who have been on a benefit for 6 months or more, and 16 to 19-year-olds
who are in industry training.
Not only is it discriminatory and retrogra de to do this, it is nonsensical, because
where is the incentive for young people on a bene fit to move into paid work if they will
not get even the minimum wage when they do ? How is it fair for a 16 or 17-year-old to
have to go back to subsistence minimum wage rates if they move to a new employer,
even if they had been paid at the full ad ult minimum wage for months, even years? If
they start a new job, they have to go bac k. How does that make sense? What we will
actually see are young people who are take n on for 90 days under the 90-day trial
period. When they finish that 90 days, they will be flicked on to a new employer, and
many of them will be locked into these low wages for much longer than 6 months,
because they cannot get a foot in the door.
This bill reinforces New Zealand as a lo w-wage economy. It will help to keep wages
down, not just for young people, but actually for all workers, and subsidise employers.
But, worst of all, I think it sends a terrible message to young people about the value that
we in this Parliament place on them. It says that they are not worth as much as older
New Zealanders, that their skil ls and their labour are less va luable, that their expenses
21 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8869
and their costs are not as important, and, e ssentially, that they as human beings are
simply not as important as older New Zealanders. It is no wonder that with a Parliament
that sends that message, young people are turnin g away from us in droves, Mr Bridges.
As I said in the second reading last week, there was a glimmer of hope last week when
we passed the second reading of the Marr iage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment
Bill. We threatened to look relevant an d interesting to young people for about 5
minutes, and the galleries were full of young people, but we have completely
undermined that message this week with th e passage of this bi ll. It tells young people
they are not worthy of our resp ect, and, as I said last week in Parliament, I am ashamed
of this House for passing it.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: We have heard from both the Labour Party
and the Greens about people leaving in drove s to go to Australia. Well, I ask members
of this House: why? Mining—mining and the opportunities that mining brings. Yet both
those parties in the last debate voted against the very bill, the Crown Minerals
(Permitting and Crown Land) Bill, that will open up the opportunities for people here in
New Zealand. So it is a little bit rich when those members get up on that moral high
ground that they seem to think they should occupy and start voting against a bill like
this, the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill.
New Zealand has got some real challe nges around youth unemployment, and there
are a number of reasons for that. Two of th e primary reasons are the global financial
crisis and the economic impact of the Chri stchurch earthquakes. When the employment
market gets tough, it gets tough for employers , and the follow-on for that is employees.
Who is right at the bottom of that ladder? Unfortunately, it is young people who lack the
skills and lack the work experience, and they  are often most hard hit when times are
tough. This is not unique to this Governme nt—this is not unique at all. This is
something that you clearly s ee evidence of when times get tough, so we have to meet
that challenge. When employers are struggling, the reality is that they have to sail closer
to the breeze; their margins are less. So wh at do they do? They look at ways in which
they can be innovative and ensu re that they can produce the products that will yield the
profits that help them employ and grow their business. When you have youngsters who
lack experience, who lack the job skills, and who lack even a simple work ethic that
often only comes when people are in work, and then you ha ve employers looking to
take someone on, and on balance they have  someone who has more skills, who has a
work track record, and who has experience, the choice becomes a very easy one for an
employer. What we need to do, what is incu mbent on members in this House, is ensure
that employers have the appropr iate incentives, have the appropriate assistance, to give
those young people a chance. That is exactly what this bill is about—it is exactly what
this bill is about.
I know that members on the other side of the House agree with this, because one
Darien Fenton in 2007 was on record, on Hansard, saying this: “the  inexperience of
first-time workers or new entrants deserves  the recognition of a short period while the
new worker becomes more socialised to wor k.” They deserve the recognition of a short
period while the new worker becomes more socialised to work. Well, I thank the
member Darien Fenton for agreeing on what th is bill is about, and I commend this bill.
We have heard the Opposition saying this is classic National Party. Well, you know
what? The classic Labour Party’s failed socia list ideology is why it is there, and this
National Government is getting on with what needs to be done.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to oppose
this bill, the Minimum Wage  (Starting-out Wage) Amendm ent Bill. New Zealand First
opposes this bill because it is an out and out attack on young people—the vulnerable
young workers who are at just the beginning of  their working careers . Cheap labour is
8870 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 21 Mar 2013
not the silver bullet to create jobs, which are vanishing every day under this
Government.
More tax, lower wages—that seems to be the way of this National Government. It
has raised GST after saying th at it would not, inflicting pain on those people on fixed
incomes. Then it has gone and taxed pape r boys, another set of  young workers. And
here it is again, launching an attack on our young workers. This is obviously not a
Government that is intent on solving the bi g issues. Job creation for all New Zealanders
must be the primary focus of the Government, and this bill will not provide additional
jobs.
On this side of the House we are quite concerned for older workers. It is hard enough
for anybody over the age of 50 to get a job anyw ay, so how stable will their jobs be?
We have heard from the other side of the House that these are hard times for employers.
Mike Sabin said that. It is easy for some employers to employ young people at a far
cheaper rate, particularly in these hard times.
With this piece of legislation the Na tional Government shows how totally
disconnected it is from the harsh realities that are faced by most of our vulnerable young
workers. It is really a slap in the face to  those young workers. This  bill does not affect
just teenagers earning a bit of extra pocket money while they are living at home with
their parents. Many of them will not have fina ncial support from their families, at all.
Some of these affected people will for all intents and purposes be independent or trying
to be independent. So how are these i ndependent young people any different from
people a couple of years older than them? Will these people get a 20 percent discount on
their rent? Perhaps a 20 percen t discount on their electric ity bills? Or even their
groceries? No, they certainly will not, definitely not on their petrol.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Could be the “YoungerGold Card”.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: Perhaps we will have to have a “YoungGold Card”. You
never know—we could perhaps come up with th at. The passing of this legislation is
definitely going to make all of these people’s lives 20 per cent harder. Their living costs
are exactly the same as other, older New Zealanders’ living costs, so why is this
Government so intent on kicking young worker s into the gutter, es pecially at a time
when people are struggling? In the last year  alone we have seen the number of young
people looking for work increase  from 80,000 to 90,000—90,000 young people not in
work or any form of training. It is a r eal disgrace and a sad indictment on this
Government.
If we are not careful, New Zealand will see a bubble of young people going out into
the world without any real work experi ence. What a total waste of a young, vital
resource that we need here in  this country. I do not believ e that we should be sending
these people off to Australia in ever-increas ing numbers. This piece of legislation is not
going to help young people, despite Mr Auchinvole laughing and smiling about it. This
piece of legislation will no t encourage young people to go out and seek work. If
anything, it really encourages them to gi ve up. By the time young people have paid to
travel to work in their cars, because petrol  is not cheap, they are worse off than they
would be if they were on welfare.
So where is the incentive for these young people to try to find these nonexistent jobs?
And what exactly is the rationale for this  change? Where is the demand? Well, the
Government is claiming that the bill will cr eate more jobs, but we have not seen any
valid statistics to back up this claim. It claims that reducing the minimum wage for one
sector of the population is going to create more jobs. The truth is that this bill will not
create more jobs. It is just another hurdle for young people trying to stay afloat in these
pressing economic times. We all know that pr ices are increasing dramatically in every
21 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8871
part of the economy. With this  piece of legislation this Government is ignoring the
plight of hard-working young New Zealanders. It treats them as second-class citizens.
It is a bit like a Back to the Future  piece of legislation. We have seen it before.
Within living memory it was women who were allowed to be paid less than men for
exactly the same work, but, fortunately, those days are passed. We know that it is totally
unacceptable to pay one sector of the population a lower wage. It is illegal
discrimination. It is very concerning to s ee ideologically driven policies emerging that
would once again treat one part of the labour force worse than the rest. Youth rates will
not encourage employers to create additional jobs. It is a sad reality that under this
Government there are families who rely on thei r children working in order to be able to
make ends meet. This is the harsh r eality for many families—young people working
after school, bringing the money home so that the families can actually make ends meet.
So what good will this change bring to them? What good is it going to do? It is simply
going to make their lives harder. And, as my colleague Asenati Lole-Taylor said, M āori
and Pacific Island families will find it very, very challenging.
Before we came into this House I had th e opportunity, thanks to my colleague, to
find a good quote from someone whom we more than likely all know of. He is a very
successful businessman called Robert Bosc h. We no doubt have got dishwashers and
fridges in our homes that bear his name . He said: “I don’t pay good wages because I
have a lot of money; I have a lot of money because I pay good wages.” I think that is a
very good message there.
New Zealand First believes that all people, irrespective of age, should be given equal
pay for equal work. We believe that this G overnment is now on a ve ry slippery slope.
With this bill the Government takes another step towards a low-wage economy. If this
Government believes that reducing the minimum wage for some people will create more
jobs, perhaps it is keen to abolish it entirely. Is that part of the plan too?
New Zealand First is disappoi nted with this bill, and,  quite honestly, we cannot
support it. We have listened to the Nationa l members of the H ouse speaking, listening
for good reasons to support this legislation, but, sorry, we have not  heard any to make
us change our mind. Where is this brighter future that National promised us? We keep
looking and waiting and looking and waiting, but to no avail. The future looks very
gloomy for some people, and particularly for young people. The horizon is not bright
for them. New Zealand First will not be supporting this bill.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: I rise with pride to support the Minimum
Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill, introduced by the Minister of Labour, the
Hon Simon Bridges. My goodness me! We have  just heard from Barbara Stewart, who
is always a very pleasant person, but my goodne ss me, the response to this bill reminds
me of that line from Shakespeare: “Methinks she doth protest too much.” I cannot see
where the problem is. Where is the problem  with providing oppor tunities for young
people to get into work and off the dole?  Where is the problem with giving young
people a job, instead of being on welfare? Those members would rather they stay on
welfare. They would rather they did not have a job. Do the Labour Party or the Green
Party not like young people? Because that is the only conclusion we can come to.
Is the real reason, lurking in the depths  of the Labour Party mind, to protect the
union-established hierarchy of employment prac tice? I think that is the case. We heard
Mr Goff give it voice. We h eard Mr Goff say: “This will lead to job displacement.”
That is the real reason. Andr ew Little was right up there behind him, saying: “We’ve
got to protect existing jobs.” National does like young people and does want to help
them. This bill is pro-youth, pro-employment, and pro-opportunity. I honestly commend
it to the House. Thank you.
8872 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 21 Mar 2013

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: This day, sadly, will go down in history as the day that
the Government officially gave up on young people—the day that the National
Government officially gave up on young peopl e—and the day that the Government, the
National Government, officially gave up on th e brighter future. This bill, the Minimum
Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill, do es both of those things. It gives up on
young people. It says that they are not worthy of a fair day’s pay for a fair day’s work. It
says that this country is not going to have the brighter future that that Government
promised in two consecutive elections and still has not delivered on. This bill is the
reason why. Government members think th at actually lowering wages is the way
forward for this country. Lowering wages, fo r whatever group in ou r society that may
be, is a downward economic spiral and it is going in the wrong direction to where this
country needs to go. When wages are lowered—in this instance, for those people aged
15 to 19—workers have less money to spend. If they have less money to spend, then
there is less work in our economy. When money is not being spent, then we have fewer
jobs in our economy, not more.
I think that that is where this Government has got it so  wrong. It is a very basic
economic theory. It is not ha rd to understand. It has been proven time and time again
that a high-wage, high-ski ll economy is the way forw ard for countries like New
Zealand. When we have high wages in our c ountry, then spending occurs and the whole
economy lifts up. That is how work is created—there is a demand driven up because
people have money to spend. If people have their spending power re duced, then that is
the path to economic decline. That is exactly what this Government is up to. It has also
given up pretending that this piece of legislatio n creates jobs. Even  the Government
itself, when it started out on the first reading of this bill, argued that this was going to
create jobs. But Government members have all stopped argui ng even that, because it is
plainly ridiculous—plainly ridiculous—to k eep up the pretence that cutting wages
creates jobs. It does no  such thing. In fact, as I have  just demonstrat ed, it actually
reduces the number of jobs available in our economy.
I want to give some very real informati on to the House about where the real problem
exists. In the Waikato Times  2 days ago, on the front page, the banner headlines
screamed out to people in the Waikato “J obless fight for work”. That is the true
reflection of where that Government has got  this country. The jobless are indeed
fighting for work. What that story detaile d was that in the Waikato the number of
people on the unemployment benefit increa sed by 33 percent between September and
December last year alone—33 percent more  unemployed people in the Waikato region
just in the last 3 months of last year. If you compared those unemployment figures in
the Waikato with December 2008, there is a massive 65.9 percent more people getting
the unemployment benefit in the Waikato now  than there were in December 2008. That
is what the real problem is. It is not the amount of wages being paid to young people. It
is the absolute dearth of jobs available in  our economy. And until the Government gets
real, fixes the real problem, stops blami ng young people for their plight, and starts
looking at itself in the mirror about its lack of a plan, we  are going to continue to
struggle as a country. It is, sadly, the day that the Government gave up on young people,
and the day that the Government gave up on a brighter future for New Zealand.
I think that when the new Minister Simon Bridges came into his new role as Minister
of Labour—it was a significant promotion for him—there wa s a lot of hope that he
might bring a new, young, shiny approach to National Party policy in that portfolio. But
what this shows is that he is just following the same tired, old, lazy policies of every
National Government that has ever been in pow er in this country. Every time we have a
National Government in power—it does not ma tter what part of the economic cycle we
are in, whether we are in a recession, whether we are in good times, or whether we are
21 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8873
in the middle of that cycle—it always has the same tired, old approach, the same lazy
answer to what it wants for New Zealanders . And what it wants for New Zealanders is
low wages. It has proven that  time and time again. Every si ngle time, that has been its
formula. This time it thinks it can get away  with it under the cove r of a recession, but if
you look historically, it show s that every single time we have had a National
Government in place it has gone after workers’ wages.
This time it is using the cover of high youth unemploymen t. It says that because
young workers are overrepresented in the unemp loyment figures, therefore the solution
is to actually discriminate against them by having lower wages. Well, what is to stop
this Government from using exactly th at same theory when it comes to M āori workers,
who are also overrepresented in the unemploym ent figures? Is it going to use the same
justification? Is it going to say—

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: They should.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: That is right. That is where its argument leads us. Is it going to
say that M āori should get only 80 percent of the minimum adult wage? Because that is
exactly the argument that it is using for young people. Paci fic Island workers are also
overrepresented in the unemployment figures. Is Simon Bridges going to have the same
solution for those workers as well? Because if National applies its failed thinking for
young workers across the whole—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: It’s very different.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Simon Bridges says that it is very different. I will be interested to
know why it is very different, because the only argument that this Government is
putting forward is that it has failed young work ers. They are overrepresented in the
unemployment figures, so therefore the Govern ment has to actually lower their wages.
The Government has also spent its time talking down young people.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Oh, rubbish.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Well, according to Mike Sabin—if the Minister listened to his
contribution to this debate—they all lack skills. All 15 to 19-year-olds lack skills.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: I didn’t say “all”.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Well, now he is saying that he didn’t say “all”, but the only thing
he had to say about young workers and their contribution to the workplace was to
denigrate them, say that they lack skills, and say that they lack experience.
The Government has no understanding of the value of young people. That is why it is
quite happy for the youth of this country to be exported to places like Australia, because
it does not understand the value of young workers to this country, to their families, and
to this economy. It is no wonder we are losing our brightest and best—our young, bright
future—to Australia. That is where they ar e headed under this Government. This piece
of legislation will make that departure happe n at much faster rates. Families will lose
their young people to Australia because there is no brighter  future for them in New
Zealand under a National Government.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: It is a great pleasure to take a brief call in the third
reading of the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill. This is a bill that
improves the chances of our young people to ga in skills. It improves the chances of our
young people to gain experience. It improve s the chances of our young people to earn
money, find a sense of purpose and a feeling of belonging, and find the dignity of work.
We do have challenges around youth unemploym ent, which we are addressing at a
number of levels. Youth unemployment is una cceptably high for this Government, and
we are working in many different areas to  bring it down. Looking at the global picture,
of course, we are doing a lot better than most econom ies around the world. Recent
figures that came out just today add emphasis to that fact, coupled with the imprimatur
of the IMF just a few days earlier about how this economy is tracking.
8874 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 21 Mar 2013
The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment suggested that this bill will
help 2,000 sixteen to 19-year-olds into the workforce in the next 2 years—2,000 more
of our young people in work. I commend my colleague Chris Auchinvole’s comment
and will repeat it for the House.  This bill is pro-youth. This b ill is pro-work. This bill is
pro-opportunity. I commend it to the House.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Split call—5 minutes.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour—Māngere): I rise to give a short contribution to the
third reading of this bill, the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill.
Three words came to mind when listening to the speech from Cam Calder, before me,
and they are “humbug”, “poppycock”, and “not true”. Labour believes in the dignity of
work. We in this party here believe also in the living wage, an d because this bill
undermines the living wage and because this  bill attacks the dignity of work, Labour
opposes this bill.
Māngere, my electorate, has the youngest  population of any other community
throughout New Zealand. With 30.4 percent of our people ag ed 15 years and under, we
are ranked No. 1. If you add the age group of 15 to 19-year-olds, th at whole collective
becomes 39 percent. For that reason I promote M āngere as the gateway to the nation,
the land of the young, beautiful, and gifted. Th at statement expresses a desire by our
parents that we have great hope for our young people. We see them as the future leaders
of this particular country. For that reason, Labour has a plan that is different from what
this Government proposes. We want to pr oduce the future leaders of this country
through education, through skills developm ent, through opportuni ties, and through
higher wages—not the kind of future this Government is building for our young people.
Government members want our young people to  become used to second-best rates.
They want our young people to become used to  low wages. Labour’s plan is to create
wealth through innovation, to ensure that our young people are earning while they are
learning. New Zealand parents right now are doing it tough under this particular
Government. The future is bleak for ha rd-working families across this nation, the
majority of them wanting to believe what they were promised—the brighter future.
But, alas, 72,000 young Kiwis aged between 18 and 30 have left this country for
Australia because they see th at as the country of opportuni ty, the country where they
can get ahead while this Government is here. It promised all of New Zealand a brighter
future. I want to ask Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga and Alfred Ngaro: where is the brighter
future in paying workers low wages? Where is the brighter future for Pacific
communities when those members continue to support low wages for workers? I do not
hear a response from that side, so they ar e content to drive wages below. They are
content to make sure that our young people— the future of this country—become used
to low pay and second-best.
Since this Government has come into pow er it has presided over the worst economic
period in 51 years, the worst and highest unemployment numbers in 13 years, and
175,000 people without jobs. The report of the Salvation Army that was released not too
long ago identified that we have got peopl e who are on the unemployment benefit and
cannot find jobs, because this Government continues to sit on its hands. The future for
New Zealand families has to be about high-value jobs, it has to be about full
employment, even, it has to be about skills, and it has to be about high wages. John Key
has failed our young people. John Key has failed to deliver for young people—30,000
under-20-year-olds are not in e ducation, not in employment, a nd not in training. That is
more than 4,000 since that Government came  into power, and if we include the age
group of 20 to 24-year-olds,  that becomes 90,000 people not in education, not in
employment, and not in training. The Government simply acknowledging that there is a
problem is not fixing it. It has got to fix it. It  has got to fix it, but it is content to drive
21 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8875
wages down. It is not prepared to do anything, so Mr Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga, where is the
brighter—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Point of order, Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga. The member’s time
has expired, but there is a point of order.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. I know the sound system is not work ing, but we are not far from Mr Sio. He
does not need to shout in this Chamber in or der to get a little bi t of attention for the
man. So, please, just—

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Deputy Speaker. Ng ā mihi nui ki a
koutou. Kia ora. It is good that  this House is looking at yo uth unemployment. It is the
right question that we are asking, but what we  have in front of us, the Minimum Wage
(Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill, is clearly the wrong answer.
I am proud to stand to oppose this bill—this flawed, ideological, and discriminatory
bill. It is flawed because the entire pr emise is wrong. Cutting wages does not create
jobs. Cutting wages does not encourage people into work. I have not heard a single
economic report or a single piece of ec onomic research being quoted by the
Government members. The fact is that there is  limited research. In fact, the research is
strongly in the other side of the camp, which says that higher wages do encourage work.
We saw it in New Zealand when the Green Party ended discrimina tory youth rates in
the mid-2000s, and it had no impact. If anyt hing, more young people were in work. So
it is flawed, the premise is wrong, and it is ideological.
We know it is plainly ideological, because  the regulatory impact statement says as
much, and because there were no alternatives canvassed by officials. It is ideological,
because it is 1990s thinking in 2013. The G overnment’s whole plan for the economy is
to cut wages and to make us even more of a low-wage, high-work economy. Mr English
said as much on competitiveness. John Key said he would be fine with seeing wages
drop.
This is not the way to build our jobs and our economy. All it is doing is ideologically
supporting a small—and I mean a very small—number of some employers who see
their future in cutting wages and flicking worker s off. It is flawed, it is ideological, and
it is discriminatory. It is cl early discriminatory because it is picking on one group. This
bill targets 16 to 17-year-olds and sets up two types of employment in New Zealand:
those 16 and 17-year-olds who are paid a discriminatory rate, and those 18 and 19-year-
olds who have been on the benefit and will also get a discriminatory rate. So it is
flawed, ideological, and discriminatory.
In fact, I would call it nasty. The Government  did not look at the alternatives, and
now we know from an Official Information Ac t request, as well, that  even the Ministry
of Education advised against it because it  is contrary to the Government’s own
education goals. But I would also contend th at from the Government’s perspective it is
counter-productive, because this sends a terrible message to  young people that they are
second-class citizens who shoul d be earning less. It sends a message to employers to
flick off young people after 90 days so that th ey can keep paying their workers at the
discriminatory lower rate. But also for all New Zealand workers, be they aged under 20
years or above, it is driving down wages across the entire New Zealand economy.
Again it goes back to that flawed a pproach to the economy. The way to build
prosperity and growth in jobs is not about reducing wages and working conditions
through 90-day trials and picki ng on paper boys and paper girl s, as in the last Budget,
and it is not about damaging the environment and racing other countries to see who can
cram as many cows as possible in a paddock. That is not our future. That is not a way to
8876 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 21 Mar 2013
provide solutions for the 90,000 young people  who are right now, today, not in
employment or training—at similar rates to Spain and other countries.
What young Kiwis and our economy need is a plan for jobs, a plan for sustainable
prosperity. Every week we get bad news. We see Mainzea l Property and Construction
and Solid Energy—and Telecom might be on the cusp of losing 1,500 jobs. We have
lost 30,000-plus jobs in manuf acturing. Kiwis want to hope. They want a vision. They
want a plan. That is what we went with to  the election in 2012: a plan to create 100,000
green jobs. This is the way the future is goi ng. This is where capit al investment trends
are going. It is what the influential business leaders are saying. They said we could see
50,000 jobs in clean energy.
I was at the Wind Energy Association c onference last night. Its plan for 3,500
megawatts of wind electricity would deli ver 1,500 jobs for New Zealand. What we
know from the oil and gas repo rt—the industry Minister Bridges was quite happy to
subsidise to the tune of $130,000—was that this  industry could see, in the most likely
scenario, 199 jobs. Yet this region lost 910 jobs in the first 3 years of this Government.
Under National we are going backwards. Kiwi s want real solutions. That is why we
are working with Labour and the other part ies on the manufacturing inquiry. That is
why we are supporting employe rs and exporters. That is why we are promoting
information and communications, which was up 17 percent in the last year. It has grown
$3 billion in the last 2 years. That is why we are putting fo rward our innovative
proposals for a second cable, gr eater training and education incentives, sensible patent
reform, and better Government procurement. And that is why we are looking at clean
energy options and the 50,000 jobs we are seeing there, and the $600 million we could
be saving per annum, and the Greenpeace report—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s time has expired.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): “More good news” was, I think, a
phrase that my colleagues in a previous generation used to say. The Minimum Wage
(Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill is good ne ws, and why it is good news is because
National believes in young people. People lis tening out there today would have been
hearing all these terrible things about youth. In fact, it was not National saying any of it;
it has been the Opposition. National belie ves in young people. Young people in New
Zealand, we believe you have an opportunity. We believe you can develop the skills and
develop the experience to be a positive co ntributor to this country. You know what?
This National Government is not going to ke ep obstacles in the way. If providing a
slightly lower wage allows an employer to make the choice of you, a young person,
over another, then, yes, this Government is prepared to back you.
This is a positive bill. This is good news. Young people of New Zealand, this is an
opportunity that the Government is providi ng for employers to employ you—sorry, not
you, Mr Deputy Speaker, but youth; yes, let us put a “t” and an “h” at the end of that—
and to actually get an opportunity over 6 months. I pointed out the other day when we
went through the Committee stage that the Opposition was attempting to argue from
principle, but it, of course, has its own youth—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Who chose that tie?
SIMON O’CONNOR : I believe you might have a similar one, Chris; maybe we
could have a cross-party discussion here . This is an opportunity, though, for young
people. We believe in young people. We believe  they should get into jobs. We want to
support them. I commend this bill to the House.
21 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8877
A party vote was called for on the question, That the Minimum Wage (Starting-out
Wage) Amendment Bill be now read a third time.
