Mana 1; Independent: Horan.
Bill read a third time.
Second Reading
Hon CHESTER BORROWS (Associate Mi nister for Social Development) on
behalf of the Minister for Social Development: I move, That the Families Commission
Amendment Bill be now read a second time . This bill amends the Families Commission
Act 2003 and is part of the process designe d to refocus the Families Commission in
order to make it a more re levant, effective, and efficient organisation. We are
streamlining the commission’s core activ ities through a leaner and more focused
structure, as part of our c onfidence and supply agreement w ith United Future. I wish to
thank it them for its contributions and these changes.
The changes provided for in the bill are relatively straightforward and can be
summarised as follows. Firs t, the commission will acquire  a new monitoring, research,
and evaluation function. This will encompass the whole social sector and be separate
from the commission’s current main function of  advocating for families. Under this, the
commission will identify evidence and resear ch that will assist in determining or
achieving the Government’s policies and priori ties in the social sector. The commission
will also play a role in coordinating rese arch and evaluation across the wider social
sector.
Second, the bill changes the commission’s governance structure by removing the title
“commissioner” from all but one member of the commission, who will be known as the
Families Commissioner. It puts the commissi on on the same footing as most other
Crown entities, and will ensure a more focu sed structure. Thirdly, the bill also provides
for the creation of a social science experts panel. This group will complement the work
of the commission’s board, and provide guida nce and academic peer review of research
undertaken by or for the commission. This will ensure that all research is rigorous and
credible. Finally, the bill will  require that the commission  prepares and publishes an
annual family status report. This will pr ovide a means by which the well-being of New
Zealand families can be regularly measured and monitored.
I would like to thank the Social Servic es Committee for its thorough and careful
attention to this bill. A total of 11 submi ssions were received on the bill. A number of
submitters were positive about the new model of the Families Commission. The
Salvation Army, the National Council of Wo men, and the IHC all support the changes
and the new function for monitoring, research , and evaluation. The IHC pointed to the
huge potential advantage of the new—to  be known—SuPERU database to avoid
research silos, and the Salvation Army is particularly interested in joining projects in
partnership with the Families Commission.
There have been some recommended technical amendments from the Social Services
Committee, and the committee recommended in cluding new clauses 4A and 9A. This
addresses some submitters’ concerns based on a misinterpretation of the bill’s
provisions and relevant Crown entity legisla tion. These clauses make it clear that the
8878 Families Commission Amendment Bill 21 Mar 2013
autonomy of the commission as prescribed  in the Crown Entities Act 2004 remains
unchanged.
The committee also recommended changes to  new section 8A in clause 7. These
changes make it clear that the commission is to  actively “identify evidence and research
that will assist in determining or achievin g the Government’s policies and priorities in
the social sector.” Other changes make it clear that in carrying out its monitoring,
evaluation, and research functions, the co mmission must act independently of the
programmes and interventions being monitored or evaluated. This is an area where I
believe the commission can add real value.
Finally, I wish to comment on the pot ential of the new SuPERU unit—the
monitoring, research, and evaluation arm of the Families Commission. If we—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I thought Subaru was a type of car.

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: It has got the wheels, buddy, to do the business. If
we are going to make a difference for the families who are struggling, we need to be
able to invest in interventions that we  know will work. This new unit will build a body
of evidence that will allow policy make rs, NGOs, and anyone wanting to invest in
social services to make informed decisions about which programmes are effective for
New Zealand families, which will add real value to the way that we all work together. I
commend the bill to the House.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour—M āngere): I am happy to rise to give this
contribution on the second reading of the Families Commission Amendment Bill. I want
to acknowledge the contribution of my colleag ues on the Social Services Committee. In
particular, I acknowledge Jacinda Ardern and Dr Rajen Prasad, because it was those two
who took the lead in Labour’s contributi on as this bill was analysed through the
committee.
As the Associate Minister for Social Development the Hon Chester Borrows said,
this bill seeks to amend the Families Commission Act 2003 to make a number of
changes to the role and operation of the commission, with the aim of improving
decision making in the social sector. Labour s upported the first reading of this bill. We
wanted it to go to the select committee as we wanted to look closely at the implications
of the bill and give the wider community the opportunity to make its submissions and to
raise its concerns on this matter.
We understand that one member of the commission would be appointed by the
Minister for Social Development as Families Commissioner, while the remaining
members would remain members without being appointed commissioners, as they are at
present. The Families Commission members would continue to comprise the board. The
restructure would include the establishment of  a social science experts panel to provide
guidance and academic peer review of any research undertaken by, and on behalf of, the
commission. The commission would also be  given a new monitoring, evaluation, and
research function, which would require it to  determine where evidence and research
would help decide, or achieve, Government priorities and to co mmission research and
manage research contracts in the social se ctor. The commission would also be required
to prepare and publish an annual Families Status Report, which would measure and
monitor the well-being of New Zealand familie s. It would also be given access by the
Government Statistician to individual schedules for research or statistical purposes.
After the select committee process, and in  consideration of what we heard from
submitters, Labour now opposes this bill. Labour believes that the changes proposed to
the commission in this bill continue an agenda to fundamentally alter its nature so that it
becomes something close to a Government depa rtment or ministry, rather than being an
autonomous Crown entity. These changes, in our view, compro mise the commission
and will limit its independence and ability to advocate effectively for families. Given
21 Mar 2013 Families Commission Amendment Bill 8879
these changes, Labour stands by its polic y of disestablishi ng the commission and,
instead, establishing a minist ry for children to focus on policies and programmes that
place children and families at the centre of all policy and ensure their interests are
paramount.
I think that when we considered the signi ficant submissions that came from the
public, the one that stood out in my mind was the submission by the Salvation Army,
and, more particularly, it wa s reaffirmed in its report She’ll be Right . One cannot help
but recognise that we have a huge problem amongst the children of New Zealand. In
fact, the figures show that unless we activel y have the political will to address the
poverty that is experienced by many families, we are just not going to get on top of it.
So, in Labour’s view, establishing a ministry  for children would enable a greater focus
of energy, resourcing, and politic al will in attempting to addr ess this issue, recognising
that the issue of the safety and the well-being  of our children has to be a priority for the
long term.
This bill before us limits the advocacy f unction of the commission and establishes a
centre for family and wh ānau knowledge within the commission to focus on
consultations and advocacy. It is unclear to us why Peter Dunne is supporting this bill,
given that the Government is curbing th e role and independent nature of the
commission. The funding for th is function is predetermined at $3.8 million per annum,
but this centre is given the additional function of producing an annual Families Status
Report, which measures and monitors the well-being of New Zealand families.
Arguably, this could be done by the Ministry of Social Development. This function is
likely to be the dominant focus of the comm ission’s advocacy function and will take up
a big chunk of the funding if it is done well. It is likely that there will be little focus on
the more general advocacy role of the commission. The amendment bill stipulates that
the commission’s consultations with familie s will be limited to its advocacy functions.
Hence its research and evaluation function wi ll not benefit from the views of family
generally.
The bill also establishes a social policy evaluation and research  unit within the
commission, with a predetermined a nnual budget of $3.55 million. This unit will
provide independent monitoring and evaluatio n of programmes and intervention in the
social sector, and provide research into key issues, programmes,  and interventions
across the sector. This section has the addi tional functions of identifying opportunities
where evidence of research will assist in ach ieving the Government’s priorities in the
social sector, commissioning research on behalf of the Government, and managing
contracts—again, on behalf of Government. Th is will be closely linked to what the
Government is doing and thus eliminate the independence of the commission to
undertake research it considers necessary—f or example, research into poverty and
financial literacy, research into  paid parental leave, and re search into family violence:
research into all the areas that our community has identified are important in order for
us to address this issue adequately.
The bill significantly alters the governan ce arrangements of the commission. There
will be only one Families Commissioner, who will not necessarily be the chair of the
board of the Families Commission. Others on the board will be members. The functions
of the Families Commission will be determined by the board. The chief executive
officer position is retained. In addition, a so cial science experts panel will be appointed
by the Minister and the Prime Minister’s Ch ief Science Advisor to peer review the
commission’s evaluation and provide advi ce. Currently the commission uses peer
reviewers from universities, ot her research centres, and i ndependent experts. It is
difficult to see how a panel of four people can peer review the range of research that
might be undertaken. Once again, argua bly, the commission will be acting like a
8880 Families Commission Amendment Bill 21 Mar 2013
Government department or ministry, focusing on the issues that the Government
considers important. We question the need for this.
This is, in our view, a confused governance structure. The power effectively lies with
its chief executive, as the Families Commissione r’s sole role is redundant. It is unclear
who will set the work programme for the co mmission: the Minister, the Government,
the advisory panel, the Families Commissioner, the chief executive, or the senior staff
of the commission. The advocacy functions of  the commission will be seriously limited
as it will be preoccupied with reporting annually on the state of families. This is
something the social report used to do yearly, and which will be produced only every 3
years.
Recently there was an example where my colleague Sue Moroney promoted a very
successful campaign around paid parental l eave—a campaign that was picked up and
supported by the majority of New Zealanders, which this Government does not like. But
the commission abandoned its role as an in dependent commission and agreed with the
Government on paid parental leave solely  based on the economic cost rather than
evidence-based policy assessment.
That gives you an example that this Government, rather than allowing the
commission to independently provide evid ence-based advice—as the commission was
set up to do—wants to be able  to control the commission. I think the Government is on
the wrong path. The right path is the La bour Party policy of disestablishing the
commission and establishing instead a mini stry for children. That then gives the
Government and us—this House—a greater focus of energy and resources on
addressing the issues of children.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: Thank you for the
opportunity to speak; I thought that guy woul d be speaking until 7 tonight, but I thank
Su’a William Sio for his contribution. I just want  to say that it is a pleasure to rise to
speak on this second reading of the Familie s Commission Amendment Bill. I just want
to, first, thank the Minister for Social De velopment, the Hon Paula Bennett. Yesterday
we acknowledged her role and her legacy in terms of the welfare reforms that she has
brought to this Parliament, which will ha ve a huge positive impact on our country.
Today we are going to acknowledge her contri bution in terms of this legislation,
because the Families Commission is about to undergo a welcome transformation.
The reason it will be transformed is that this Government, this National
Government, believes in better, more effec tive public services. What does that mean?
What are we going to do? Well, the Associat e Minister for Social Development Chester
Borrows touched on it earlier. We are restructuring the commission because this will
see its core activities streamlined into a leaner, more focused structure. It will be headed
by a single commissioner, and the search for that single commissioner is going on as we
speak. The number of commissioners will go down from the original number of seven.
That is right—less bureaucracy  in one fell swoop. It  will be governed by a board, and
the board will include Professor Sir Peter Gluckman. It will also have public sector,
philanthropic, and business representatives, and it will give credible community input
into—[Interruption] Oh! Asenati Lole-Taylor knows this—the direction of an important
entity in our Government.
For the benefit of Parliament, I say that ye sterday we had the financial review of the
Families Commission. We had some valuable contributions from the acting chairman
and the acting chief executive officer, as well as Sir Peter, who turned up to elaborate on
the future of this commission.
The commission will also commission and cont ract social sector research on topics
referred by the Government. I know my colleague Su’a William Sio referred to the lack
of independence, but it really  is important that some of  the research done actually
21 Mar 2013 Families Commission Amendment Bill 8881
becomes implemented and becomes part of the Budget-setting process for the
Government, so that those things can make a differen ce to people out in our
communities. There is no point in having rese arch sitting on a sh elf in the Wellington
office of some policy analyst in one of the Government de partments. It is really
important that we have this type of resear ch out in the open, read by many, distributed
across many sectors, and implemented by thos e who are able to do the implementation,
which includes Government officials and poli ticians alike. So the commission will take
on a new role providing independent monitori ng, evaluation, and research to measure
the effectiveness of initiatives across our social sector.
Labour doubts this, but we we re left in no doubt on this  side of the House by the
testimony of Sir Peter Gluckman yesterday at  the financial review that it is about
independence. It is about evidence-based research that will be implemented in our
communities through policy. So funding will be  reduced from $32 million over 4 years
to $28 million, and $14 million will be repriori tised for the social policy evaluation and
research unit, which some people call SuPERU.
Before I finish my contribution tonight I just want to touch on the recommendations
of the Social Services Committee, which the Minister also alluded to. I want to thank all
the members of the committee for their contri butions, Dr Prasad and those across the
aisle, and also my colleagues, like Alfred  Ngaro and Melissa Lee,  who is the deputy
chair, and the other members of our committee. Even though there were a small number
of submitters—there were 11—we actually gleaned quite a bit of feedback and we made
certain adjustments. Also, I want to acknowle dge our officials, pa rliamentary counsel,
and our clerks, who were also part of the team, if you like, that brought these
recommendations back to the House. I want to acknowledge them, and they are with us
here tonight.
Just very quickly, we are amending clause 11 to ensure that the social science experts
panel will comprise a minimum of four members—a minimum of four, Su’a. I know he
criticised the figure, but it is a minimum of  four members, and we changed it to allow
for a degree of flexibility to appoint additional members if required. So we have
allowed for that degree of flex ibility in our recommendations. It is also about amending
clause 11 to ensure that th e panel would come under approp riate provisions pertaining
to the appointment and payment of members, conflicts of interest, indemnities, and
insurance. So that is another important addition to the bill as presented to the House at
its first reading.
The Minister referred to amending clause  7. It is really about correcting the
misconception that the commission will merely identify opportunities for evaluation and
research. It will be actively identifying these opportunities. I think that is an important
consideration when we move fo rward in terms of those subjects that will be identified.
Yesterday the commission went through some  of those. Some involved improving the
achievement levels of M āori and Pasifika children. Th ere is a whole host of these
subjects that it is seeing as priorities going forward. If we are going to make a difference
for the families in this country, Aotearoa New Zealand, who are struggling, we need to
be able to invest in interventions that we know will work.
The body of evidence that wi ll come out of this commission will allow policy
makers, service providers, politicians, and anyone wanting to inve st in our social
services to make better, more informed deci sions. It is about having an evidence base,
as Sir Peter Gluckman referred to at our fi nancial review of the commission yesterday.
It is about those evidence-based interven tions that produce better long-term outcomes
for our families, our communities, and, ultimately, our nation. That is why I support this
bill.
8882 Families Commission Amendment Bill 21 Mar 2013

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: I am very interested in  what the member opposite,
Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga, has just said. The member talked about the legacy of the Minister
for Social Development. It is very inte resting that we had the Families Commission
before the Social Services Committee yest erday, and now we are talking about this
legacy. Let me tell the chairman  of that committee that th ere is daylight between how
the Minister conceives this commission and how the commission presented itself
yesterday. There is daylight in that—absol ute daylight. Just putting a small number of
very well-known researchers on to the commission will not make an efficient
commission in the sense that the Minister thinks it will.
Let us take just one of the things that th is Minister is presiding over, and I look
forward to hearing what the explanations  are. Yesterday we found out about the
commission in this manifestation sp ending $411,000 on one staff member for 17

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: That sounds like the sort of thing that used to happen under the
Labour Government.

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: Is the member supporting th is? Is the Hon Mr Bridges
supporting this? Because if the member is, then  that Government ha s got a lot of work
to do to find out about all of the consultant s who are being used. That is what this
commission has been driven to: bringing people from Australia, who then establish their
own consultancy company, and then their own consultancy company gets hired—hiring
the same person back to the commission and spending $411,000. That is what this
Minister is presiding over at  the moment. I know there have  been some justifications
such as “We’ve been restructuring.” and “W e’ve been having a look to see.” Well, why
is this commission not developing the capaci ty within the commission? It is not. So
there is daylight between what the legacy of this Minister will  be and what this
commission is set up to do.
There is also daylight between how the Mini ster conceives of the research functions
of this commission and how the commissioners  described it yesterday. At the moment,
it seems it will end up being probably not too different from what it has been evolving
to, yet the Minister has couched this in te rms of this radical differentiation between
what the commission has been set up to do a nd where she wants it to go. There will not
be much difference. There will still be largely—[Interruption] Three million dollars, Mr
Bridges, will not give you the kind of research  that this Minister wants. The Minister
talks about evidence-based research. Ther e is daylight between evidence-based
research—that Government is not using the ev idence that is currently available. On the
“boot camps” legislation, the research says do not do it. The Minister did it. It is not
working. Mr Bridges might like  to know about this. It is the same with the welfare
reforms that we debated yesterday. The English experience and evidence show that
those kinds of sanctions do not work. But, no, the Minister wants to do it. So why is
there this daylight between the Minister’s policies—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: How much will it cost?

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: —in the area of the most vul nerable in our society and the
work of the commission, trying  to set it up to do the evidential work that it will do? It
will produce the reports, and I bet you this Government will not put them into operation.
That is what will happen. So now there is  this daylight. What is the question the
member is asking about costs?

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: How much will it cost?

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: Well, all that your Government is giving for this role,
Minister, is $3 million. It cannot be done—cannot be done.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 6 p.m.

Economic Growth—GDP Growth for December 2012 Quarter and Unemployment 
1. DAVID BENNETT (National—Hamilton East)  to the Minister of Finance : 
What reports has he received on the economy? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Actin g Minister of Finance) : Today Statistics New 
Zealand has released the gross domestic pr oduct data for the D ecember 2012 quarter. It 
shows that the New Zealand economy grew 1.5 percent in the quarter—the highest 
quarterly growth since December 2009 and ab ove market expectations. Annual growth 
was 3 percent year on year. The last time this was higher was before the global financial 
8830 Questions for Oral Answer 21 Mar 2013 
crisis and before the domestic recession that  preceded that crisis. This is a reasonably 
encouraging result, particul arly when New Zealand’s 3 percent growth in 2012 is 
compared with other countries: 1.6 percent in the US, 1.1 percent in Canada, 0.4 percent 
in Japan, 0.3 percent in the UK, and negative 0.9 percent in the euro area.  
David Bennett: What are the main drivers of GDP growth in the December quarter?  
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: Statistics New Zealand reports broad growth, with 15 of the 
16 measured industries growing in the December quarter. The main drivers of growth in 
the December quarter were forestry, which grew 9 percent, the largest increase since 
1999; retail accommodation and restaurants, up 2.3 percent, driven by retail activity; 
wholesale trade, up 2.1 percent, driven by equipment and machinery sales; and 
construction activity, up 1.8 percent, which was the fifth consecutive quarterly increase. 
Manufacturing activity in the December quarter was up 2.7 percent year on year, but 
down 0.5 percent in the quarter, and that wa s mainly due to a fall in oil production. 
Household consumption increased 1.6 percent, and exports increased 2.1 percent.  
David Bennett: What is the outlook for New Ze aland’s economic growth, and how 
does that compare with other developed countries?  
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Treasury and the Reserve Bank forecast that New 
Zealand’s economy can expect growth of 2 to 3 percent per year over the next 4 years. 
This is in spite of the headwinds of ongoing uncertainty in the world economy, an 
elevated exchange rate, deleveraging in th e household and Government sectors, and, of 
course, this year’s drought. New Zealand’s forecast growth is higher than consensus 
forecasts for the eurozone, Japan, the United Kingdom, and Canada. It is in line with 
forecast growth in the United States of Amer ica and slightly below that of Australia. 
There remains work to do, but this shows that New Zealand is broadly heading in the 
right economic direction.  
David Bennett: What are the risks to growth in th e next few years, and what steps is 
the Government taking to manage these risks?  
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Although the world economy is showing some positive 
signs, recent events in Europe and questio ns about the process of unwinding central 
bank balance sheets shows th at some uncertainty does remain. That is why the 
Government has focused on developing its Business Growth Agenda, a comprehensive 
plan for building a productive and competitive economy and encouraging business 
investment and growth, and also raising nati onal savings by getting back into surplus, 
and developing new financial stability t ools, which include the macro-prudential 
framework.  
Hon David Parker : Why is the Minister claiming the economy is performing well, 
given that 23,000 people lost their jobs and 33,000 people left the workforce in the very 
same December quarter that he has been referring to?  
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: It is worth pointing out to the member that, actually, in the

CROWN MINERALS (PERMITTING AND CROWN LAND) BILL 
Second Reading 
Hon SIMON BRIDGES (Minister of Energy and Resources) : I move, That the 
Crown Minerals (Permitting and Crown Land) Bill be now read a second time . I would 
like to take this opportunity to thank the chair, Jonath an Young, and members of the 
Commerce Committee for their work in consider ing this complex piece of legislation. I 
also acknowledge the time submitters took to provide their views to the select 
committee. It is positive that the select committee had the opportunity to hear views 
about mining from so many perspectives.  
This bill refreshes the Cr own Minerals Act 1991 to support the Government’s 
objective of growing the mineral sector whilst ensuring even greater levels of health and 
safety and environmental oversight. New Zealanders rightly demand high standards 
from the mining sector. This legislation is a key element in providing that assurance. 
This bill does not seek to repl ace existing legislation in relation to health and safety and 
environmental management; rather, it bett er integrates the f unctions of various 
regulatory processes to ensure health and sa fety and environmental considerations are 
embedded throughout the process. The majority of submitters agreed with the proposal 
to consider the health and safety and environmental capacity of permit applicants before 
permits are awarded. Processes to ensure these matters remain on the agenda for the life 
cycle of a permit, such as annual review m eetings with permit holders and information-
sharing provisions between re gulators, were also endorsed. I am confident that the 
Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment will implement these changes in a 
way that does not result in undue delay in permit decisions or duplication of effort.  
The report of the Royal Commission on th e Pike River Coal Mine Tragedy was 
released while the bill was being consid ered by the select committee. The royal 
commission explicitly endorsed the proposals put forward in the review of the Crown 
Minerals Act, but it was clear that these need ed to be strengthened. The bill as reported 
back incorporates further amendments th at take account of th e royal commission’s 
report and submissions that were heard on th is. These changes will ensure that health 
and safety becomes an integral part of the permitting process, without introducing 
undue costs or uncertainty. This bill represents the Government’s response to two of the 
royal commission’s recommendations. A comp rehensive work programme on the other 
14 recommendations is under way.  
As expected, the purpose statement gene rated a significant amount of interest 
throughout the committee’s proceedings. The purpose statement neatly encapsulated the 
Government’s desires for the sector. It intentionally promotes “prospecting for, 
exploration for, and mining of Crown owned minerals for the benefit of New Zealand,” 
but recognises that any activity must be undertaken in accordan ce with “good industry 
practice”. Embedding such a balance into the purpose statement makes it clear that 
permitting decisions will consider health a nd safety matters as well as the potential 
economic return to the Crown.  
This bill ensures the ongoi ng protection of schedule 4 land. This protection is 
enhanced by automatically including any land that meets the criteria for inclusion in 
schedule 4. Some concerns were raised that  having Cabinet as the decision maker for 
the designation of high-value conservati on land would erode the Minister of 
Conservation’s role as steward of the conser vation estate. This is not the case. It has 
21 Mar 2013 Crown Minerals (Permitting and Crown Land) Bill 8845 
always been a matter for Cabinet to add la nd into schedule 4. The reforms ensure that 
this will happen as a matter of course. Th ere was some objection to the Minister of 
Energy and Resources having a role in dete rmining whether to grant access to Crown 
conservation land for mining and the inclusion of economic criteria in the decision into 
whether to grant a land access agreement. Th e bill retains these proposals, but ensures 
that the role of the Minister  of Energy and Resources is limited to the small number of 
mining operations that have the potential to generate a significant economic return. 
Economic considerations will also take account of any direct impacts on other 
businesses that might be affected by the mining project.  
This bill is part of a package of refo rms that responds to the Waitangi Tribunal’s 
report on the management of the petroleum resource. It introduces a requirement for 
permit holders to report annually on their engage ment with iwi and hap ū. Some 
submissions suggested that this requirement does not go far enough and that it should 
spell out detailed expectations on how permit holders should engage and the 
consequences of doing so. I am of the view th at it is a matter for permit holders and iwi 
to determine how to engage at a local le vel. Embedding such expectations into the 
legislation would be too limiting, given the diversity of iwi views on mining and their 
willingness to engage with permit holders. This requirement must be seen in the context 
of a broader range of reforms aimed at enhancing the relationships between permit 
holders, the Crown, and iwi. Of note is th e intent that New Zealand Petroleum and 
Minerals will provide operational support to assi st creating relationships at a local level 
in the interests of all parties.  
I am grateful to the submitters and the select committee, whose thorough 
consideration has served to improve this le gislation. The bill as reported back reflects 
the Commerce Committee’s agreement on the majority of amendments proposed and its 
response to issues raised by a wide range of  submitters. It also includes a large number 
of technical amendments to improve the workability of the Act and bring it into line 
with modern drafting conventions. This bill is a key element in helping New Zealand 
realise its huge petroleum and mineral potential, while giving us the confidence that the 
regulatory system we have is robust. I am very pleased to commend the Crown Minerals 
(Permitting and Crown Land) Bill to the House.

Third Reading 
Hon SIMON BRIDGES (Minister of Labour) : I move, That the Minimum Wage 
(Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill be now read a third time . It gives me great 
satisfaction to support this bi ll at its third reading. This bill delivers on the 
Government’s commitment to establish a starting- out wage to assist young people to 
gain a foothold in the labour market. I woul d like to thank the Tr ansport and Industrial 
Relations Committee, officials, and submitte rs for their work on, and contribution to, 
this bill.  
21 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8861 
The Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage ) Amendment Bill is part of the 
Government’s focus to create job oppor tunities for young people who are finding it 
difficult to get work in the current economic climate, and who have not been helped by 
the minimum wage settings broadened by the previous Government. The youth 
minimum wage was abolished in 2008 by the Labour Government and replaced by a 
new entrants wage that was rarely us ed. Research commi ssioned by the then 
Department of Labour suggests the aboliti on of the youth minimu m wage has resulted 
in the loss of up to 9,000 jobs for young Ne w Zealanders. The new entrants wage 
applies for the first 3 months or 200 cumu lative hours. Businesses complain it is too 
complicated, impractical, and fleeting to bot her with. Ministry of Business, Innovation 
and Employment research indicates it is used by only 2 percent of employers.  
The starting-out wage will encourage empl oyers to take on young people, who will 
then have the satisfaction of earning mone y, gaining skills, and getting the work 
experience they need. The bill achieves this by providing the ability to set different 
minimum wage rates, known as starting-ou t wage rates, by Order in Council for 
specified groups of young people aged 16 to 19 y ears. These rates must be set at no less 
than 80 percent of the adult minimum wage. This bill encourages continuity with the 
same employer by providing that a young pers on on a starting-out wage must complete 
6 months of continuous work with an employer before they are entitled to be paid the 
adult rate by the employer. With a steady work history behind them, young people, like 
other employees with a steady work history, will be seen as less risky for new 
employers to take on.  
The bill also addresses the problem of young people who have been on a benefit for a 
length of time of 6 months or more and may face difficulty re-entering or gaining a 
foothold in the workforce. The bill will provide for a starting-out wage rate to be set for 
these young people, and in so doing encourag e employers to take on young people who 
have been out of the workforce for a while or may lack skills or experience. The bill 
also provides for young people aged betw een 16 and 19 years w ho are required to 
undergo training as a condition of the work to be paid the starting-out wage, rather than 
the minimum training wage.  
This Government is committed to creating an environment that encourages economic 
growth. Part of this environment is providi ng a better balance to our labour market 
rules, which focuses on helping businesses grow while ensuring workers’ rights and 
opportunities are maintained. In itiatives such as the star ting-out wage will give young 
people the opportunity to get a foot in the door . This bill will provide a strong incentive 
for employers to take on young people. Once in work, young people will gain the 
essential and necessary skills and work experi ence that will assist them throughout their 
working lives. This is a positive step fo r young people in New Zealand. I commend this 
bill to the House.

Second Reading 
Hon CHESTER BORROWS (Associate Mi nister for Social Development) on 
behalf of the Minister for Social Development: I move, That the Families Commission 
Amendment Bill be now read a second time . This bill amends the Families Commission 
Act 2003 and is part of the process designe d to refocus the Families Commission in 
order to make it a more re levant, effective, and efficient organisation. We are 
streamlining the commission’s core activ ities through a leaner and more focused 
structure, as part of our c onfidence and supply agreement w ith United Future. I wish to 
thank it them for its contributions and these changes.  
The changes provided for in the bill are relatively straightforward and can be 
summarised as follows. Firs t, the commission will acquire  a new monitoring, research, 
and evaluation function. This will encompass the whole social sector and be separate 
from the commission’s current main function of  advocating for families. Under this, the 
commission will identify evidence and resear ch that will assist in determining or 
achieving the Government’s policies and priori ties in the social sector. The commission 
will also play a role in coordinating rese arch and evaluation across the wider social 
sector.  
Second, the bill changes the commission’s governance structure by removing the title 
“commissioner” from all but one member of the commission, who will be known as the 
Families Commissioner. It puts the commissi on on the same footing as most other 
Crown entities, and will ensure a more focu sed structure. Thirdly, the bill also provides 
for the creation of a social science experts panel. This group will complement the work 
of the commission’s board, and provide guida nce and academic peer review of research 
undertaken by or for the commission. This will ensure that all research is rigorous and 
credible. Finally, the bill will  require that the commission  prepares and publishes an 
annual family status report. This will pr ovide a means by which the well-being of New 
Zealand families can be regularly measured and monitored.  
I would like to thank the Social Servic es Committee for its thorough and careful 
attention to this bill. A total of 11 submi ssions were received on the bill. A number of 
submitters were positive about the new model of the Families Commission. The 
Salvation Army, the National Council of Wo men, and the IHC all support the changes 
and the new function for monitoring, research , and evaluation. The IHC pointed to the 
huge potential advantage of the new—to  be known—SuPERU database to avoid 
research silos, and the Salvation Army is particularly interested in joining projects in 
partnership with the Families Commission.  
There have been some recommended technical amendments from the Social Services 
Committee, and the committee recommended in cluding new clauses 4A and 9A. This 
addresses some submitters’ concerns based on a misinterpretation of the bill’s 
provisions and relevant Crown entity legisla tion. These clauses make it clear that the 
8878 Families Commission Amendment Bill 21 Mar 2013 
autonomy of the commission as prescribed  in the Crown Entities Act 2004 remains 
unchanged.  
The committee also recommended changes to  new section 8A in clause 7. These 
changes make it clear that the commission is to  actively “identify evidence and research

the social sector.” Other changes make it clear that in carrying out its monitoring, 
evaluation, and research functions, the co mmission must act independently of the 
programmes and interventions being monitored or evaluated. This is an area where I 
believe the commission can add real value.

monitoring, research, and evaluation arm of the Families Commission. If we—

the commission in this bill continue an agenda to fundamentally alter its nature so that it 
becomes something close to a Government depa rtment or ministry, rather than being an 
autonomous Crown entity. These changes, in our view, compro mise the commission 
and will limit its independence and ability to advocate effectively for families. Given 
21 Mar 2013 Families Commission Amendment Bill 8879 
these changes, Labour stands by its polic y of disestablishi ng the commission and, 
instead, establishing a minist ry for children to focus on policies and programmes that 
place children and families at the centre of all policy and ensure their interests are 
paramount.  
I think that when we considered the signi ficant submissions that came from the 
public, the one that stood out in my mind was the submission by the Salvation Army, 
and, more particularly, it wa s reaffirmed in its report She’ll be Right . One cannot help 
but recognise that we have a huge problem amongst the children of New Zealand. In 
fact, the figures show that unless we activel y have the political will to address the 
poverty that is experienced by many families, we are just not going to get on top of it. 
So, in Labour’s view, establishing a ministry  for children would enable a greater focus 
of energy, resourcing, and politic al will in attempting to addr ess this issue, recognising 
that the issue of the safety and the well-being  of our children has to be a priority for the 
long term.  
This bill before us limits the advocacy f unction of the commission and establishes a 
centre for family and wh ānau knowledge within the commission to focus on 
consultations and advocacy. It is unclear to us why Peter Dunne is supporting this bill, 
given that the Government is curbing th e role and independent nature of the 
commission. The funding for th is function is predetermined at $3.8 million per annum, 
but this centre is given the additional function of producing an annual Families Status 
Report, which measures and monitors the well-being of New Zealand families. 
Arguably, this could be done by the Ministry of Social Development. This function is 
likely to be the dominant focus of the comm ission’s advocacy function and will take up 
a big chunk of the funding if it is done well. It is likely that there will be little focus on 
the more general advocacy role of the commission. The amendment bill stipulates that 
the commission’s consultations with familie s will be limited to its advocacy functions. 
Hence its research and evaluation function wi ll not benefit from the views of family 
generally.  
The bill also establishes a social policy evaluation and research  unit within the 
commission, with a predetermined a nnual budget of $3.55 million. This unit will 
provide independent monitoring and evaluatio n of programmes and intervention in the 
social sector, and provide research into key issues, programmes,  and interventions 
across the sector. This section has the addi tional functions of identifying opportunities 
where evidence of research will assist in ach ieving the Government’s priorities in the 
social sector, commissioning research on behalf of the Government, and managing 
contracts—again, on behalf of Government. Th is will be closely linked to what the 
Government is doing and thus eliminate the independence of the commission to 
undertake research it considers necessary—f or example, research into poverty and 
financial literacy, research into  paid parental leave, and re search into family violence: 
research into all the areas that our community has identified are important in order for 
us to address this issue adequately.  
The bill significantly alters the governan ce arrangements of the commission. There 
will be only one Families Commissioner, who will not necessarily be the chair of the 
board of the Families Commission. Others on the board will be members. The functions 
of the Families Commission will be determined by the board. The chief executive 
officer position is retained. In addition, a so cial science experts panel will be appointed 
by the Minister and the Prime Minister’s Ch ief Science Advisor to peer review the 
commission’s evaluation and provide advi ce. Currently the commission uses peer 
reviewers from universities, ot her research centres, and i ndependent experts. It is 
difficult to see how a panel of four people can peer review the range of research that 
might be undertaken. Once again, argua bly, the commission will be acting like a 
8880 Families Commission Amendment Bill 21 Mar 2013 
Government department or ministry, focusing on the issues that the Government 
considers important. We question the need for this.  
This is, in our view, a confused governance structure. The power effectively lies with 
its chief executive, as the Families Commissione r’s sole role is redundant. It is unclear 
who will set the work programme for the co mmission: the Minister, the Government, 
the advisory panel, the Families Commissioner, the chief executive, or the senior staff 
of the commission. The advocacy functions of  the commission will be seriously limited 
as it will be preoccupied with reporting annually on the state of families. This is 
something the social report used to do yearly, and which will be produced only every 3 
years.  
Recently there was an example where my colleague Sue Moroney promoted a very 
successful campaign around paid parental l eave—a campaign that was picked up and 
supported by the majority of New Zealanders, which this Government does not like. But 
the commission abandoned its role as an in dependent commission and agreed with the 
Government on paid parental leave solely  based on the economic cost rather than 
evidence-based policy assessment.  
That gives you an example that this Government, rather than allowing the 
commission to independently provide evid ence-based advice—as the commission was 
set up to do—wants to be able  to control the commission. I think the Government is on 
the wrong path. The right path is the La bour Party policy of disestablishing the 
commission and establishing instead a mini stry for children. That then gives the 
Government and us—this House—a greater focus of energy and resources on 
addressing the issues of children. 
Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA (National—Maungakiekie) : Thank you for the 
opportunity to speak; I thought that guy woul d be speaking until 7 tonight, but I thank 
Su’a William Sio for his contribution. I just want  to say that it is a pleasure to rise to 
speak on this second reading of the Familie s Commission Amendment Bill. I just want 
to, first, thank the Minister for Social De velopment, the Hon Paula Bennett. Yesterday 
we acknowledged her role and her legacy in terms of the welfare reforms that she has 
brought to this Parliament, which will ha ve a huge positive impact on our country. 
Today we are going to acknowledge her contri bution in terms of this legislation, 
because the Families Commission is about to undergo a welcome transformation.  
 The reason it will be transformed is that this Government, this National 
Government, believes in better, more effec tive public services. What does that mean? 
What are we going to do? Well, the Associat e Minister for Social Development Chester 
Borrows touched on it earlier. We are restructuring the commission because this will 
see its core activities streamlined into a leaner, more focused structure. It will be headed 
by a single commissioner, and the search for that single commissioner is going on as we 
speak. The number of commissioners will go down from the original number of seven. 
That is right—less bureaucracy  in one fell swoop. It  will be governed by a board, and 
the board will include Professor Sir Peter Gluckman. It will also have public sector, 
philanthropic, and business representatives, and it will give credible community input 
into—[Interruption] Oh! Asenati Lole-Taylor knows this—the direction of an important 
entity in our Government.  
For the benefit of Parliament, I say that ye sterday we had the financial review of the 
Families Commission. We had some valuable contributions from the acting chairman 
and the acting chief executive officer, as well as Sir Peter, who turned up to elaborate on 
the future of this commission.  
The commission will also commission and cont ract social sector research on topics 
referred by the Government. I know my colleague Su’a William Sio referred to the lack 
of independence, but it really  is important that some of  the research done actually 
21 Mar 2013 Families Commission Amendment Bill 8881 
becomes implemented and becomes part of the Budget-setting process for the 
Government, so that those things can make a differen ce to people out in our 
communities. There is no point in having rese arch sitting on a sh elf in the Wellington 
office of some policy analyst in one of the Government de partments. It is really 
important that we have this type of resear ch out in the open, read by many, distributed 
across many sectors, and implemented by thos e who are able to do the implementation, 
which includes Government officials and poli ticians alike. So the commission will take 
on a new role providing independent monitori ng, evaluation, and research to measure 
the effectiveness of initiatives across our social sector. 
 Labour doubts this, but we we re left in no doubt on this  side of the House by the 
testimony of Sir Peter Gluckman yesterday at  the financial review that it is about 
independence. It is about evidence-based research that will be implemented in our 
communities through policy. So funding will be  reduced from $32 million over 4 years 
to $28 million, and $14 million will be repriori tised for the social policy evaluation and 
research unit, which some people call SuPERU.  
Before I finish my contribution tonight I just want to touch on the recommendations 
of the Social Services Committee, which the Minister also alluded to. I want to thank all 
the members of the committee for their contri butions, Dr Prasad and those across the 
aisle, and also my colleagues, like Alfred  Ngaro and Melissa Lee,  who is the deputy 
chair, and the other members of our committee. Even though there were a small number 
of submitters—there were 11—we actually gleaned quite a bit of feedback and we made 
certain adjustments. Also, I want to acknowle dge our officials, pa rliamentary counsel, 
and our clerks, who were also part of the team, if you like, that brought these 
recommendations back to the House. I want to acknowledge them, and they are with us 
here tonight.  
Just very quickly, we are amending clause 11 to ensure that the social science experts 
panel will comprise a minimum of four members—a minimum of four, Su’a. I know he 
criticised the figure, but it is a minimum of  four members, and we changed it to allow 
for a degree of flexibility to appoint additional members if required. So we have 
allowed for that degree of flex ibility in our recommendations. It is also about amending 
clause 11 to ensure that th e panel would come under approp riate provisions pertaining 
to the appointment and payment of members, conflicts of interest, indemnities, and 
insurance. So that is another important addition to the bill as presented to the House at 
its first reading. 
 The Minister referred to amending clause  7. It is really about correcting the 
misconception that the commission will merely identify opportunities for evaluation and 
research. It will be actively identifying these opportunities. I think that is an important 
consideration when we move fo rward in terms of those subjects that will be identified. 
Yesterday the commission went through some  of those. Some involved improving the 
achievement levels of M āori and Pasifika children. Th ere is a whole host of these 
subjects that it is seeing as priorities going forward. If we are going to make a difference 
for the families in this country, Aotearoa New Zealand, who are struggling, we need to 
be able to invest in interventions that we know will work.  
The body of evidence that wi ll come out of this commission will allow policy 
makers, service providers, politicians, and anyone wanting to inve st in our social 
services to make better, more informed deci sions. It is about having an evidence base, 
as Sir Peter Gluckman referred to at our fi nancial review of the commission yesterday. 
It is about those evidence-based interven tions that produce better long-term outcomes 
for our families, our communities, and, ultimately, our nation. That is why I support this 
bill.
